rule_text: Organizations that collect biometric data must publish a written retention schedule and destruction policy before collecting any data, and must actually destroy the data when the purpose expires or within three years, whichever comes first.
rule_text_technical: No private entity may collect, capture, purchase, receive through trade, or otherwise obtain a person's biometric identifier or biometric information unless it first develops a written policy, made available to the public, establishing a retention schedule and guidelines for permanently destroying biometric identifiers and biometric information.

first_instance.law_name: Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act, 740 ILCS 14/15(a)

instances.notes: First law globally requiring a publicly available written retention and destruction schedule before biometric data collection begins.
Storage limitation principle requires data to be kept no longer than necessary, but does not require a publicly published schedule.
Requires deletion after processing purpose is fulfilled, but no pre-collection public policy requirement.

Both require limiting data retention to legally prescribed or purpose-necessary periods, but BIPA s15a focuses specifically on biometric data with a written published policy, while this rule applies broadly to all personal data with retention tied to legislative or processing-purpose timeframes.

Both require limiting retention to the minimum period necessary for the stated purpose; PIPL applies broadly to all personal information with a general minimum-necessary standard, while BIPA requires a published retention schedule specifically for biometric data.
Both require retention schedules and destruction policies, but Qatar's rule applies to all personal data while BIPA is biometric-specific, and Qatar also emphasizes compliance with stated purposes.

instances.citation: Ch. 501, Part V, F.S. — Biometric Data (Voice and Facial Recognition — Notification)
instances.notes: Both address biometric data obligations; Florida requires affirmative notification when using voice/facial recognition while Illinois BIPA requires publishing a retention and destruction policy before collection.

rule_text: You must obtain written informed consent from a person before collecting, capturing, or otherwise obtaining their biometric identifiers or biometric information. The person must be told what is being collected, why, and for how long.
rule_text_technical: No private entity may collect, capture, purchase, receive through trade, or otherwise obtain a person's biometric identifier or biometric information unless it first informs the subject in writing of the specific purpose and length of term for which such identifier or information is being collected, stored and used, and receives a written release executed by the subject.

first_instance.law_name: Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act, 740 ILCS 14/15(b)

instances.notes: First law globally requiring affirmative written opt-in consent before any biometric data collection by a private entity.
Requires explicit consent for biometric processing as sensitive data, but allows other legal bases (employment, vital interests) and does not require written form.
Provides opt-out right for use/sharing of sensitive personal information (including biometrics) rather than opt-in consent before collection.
Requires consent for sensitive personal data including biometrics, but consent can be implied in some employment contexts.
Prohibits real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces without explicit authorisation; does not establish a general pre-collection consent rule.
Permits biometric data collection and processing for state security and social management purposes without individual consent.

Both require explicit consent before processing personal/biometric data, but BIPA s15b is specific to biometric data collection with a written consent requirement, while this rule applies broadly to all personal data processing.

Both require freely given, informed, and explicit consent before handling personal information; PIPL additionally requires new consent when purpose or method changes and applies broadly to all personal information, whereas BIPA is limited to biometric data.
Both require written informed consent before collecting/processing data, but this rule is specific to agricultural data rather than biometric data.

Both require informed consent before processing, but the Philippine DPA applies to all personal information broadly and specifies consent must be 'freely given, specific, informed, and evidenced by written, electronic, or recorded means,' whereas BIPA is specific to biometric data and requires written consent.
Both address consent validity requirements (clear, specific, freely given), but Qatar applies to all personal data while BIPA is specific to biometric data.

Both address obtaining meaningful consent with individuals understanding what data is collected, but BIPA is a binding law requiring written informed consent for biometric data specifically, while the ASEAN guide is a voluntary broader recommendation for AI data generally.

Both require informed consent from human subjects, but this rule applies broadly to all scientific and technological research participants in China and is part of an ethics review framework, while BIPA focuses specifically on biometric data collection.

instances.citation: Ch. 501, Part V, F.S. — Biometric Data (Voice and Facial Recognition — Consent)
instances.notes: Both require explicit consent before processing biometric data; Florida focuses on voice and facial recognition systems while Illinois BIPA covers all biometric data collection.
Both require obtaining written consent before collecting biometric/facial data, independently adopted under different legal systems but with the same substantive requirement.

rule_text: Organizations may not sell, lease, trade, or otherwise profit from a person's biometric data. Biometric data must not be disclosed to third parties without consent.
rule_text_technical: No private entity in possession of a biometric identifier or biometric information may sell, lease, trade, or otherwise profit from a person's or a customer's biometric identifier or biometric information.

first_instance.law_name: Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act, 740 ILCS 14/15(c)

instances.notes: First law to categorically prohibit monetisation of biometric data regardless of consent.
Purpose limitation and special category protections restrict commercial use, but do not impose a categorical sale prohibition.
Consumers can opt out of sale/sharing of sensitive personal information but no outright prohibition on selling biometrics.
Both prohibit selling or otherwise profiting from data without authorization, but this rule applies to agricultural data rather than biometric data.
Both prohibit commercial exploitation of biometric data, but this rule is specific to attendance management contexts and prohibits sharing with third parties or commercial use.

rule_text: Any person whose biometric privacy rights are violated can sue the collector directly and recover $1,000 to $5,000 per violation (plus attorney's fees) without proving actual harm. Class actions are permitted.
rule_text_technical: Any person aggrieved by a violation of BIPA shall have a right of action in a State circuit court and may recover liquidated damages of $1,000 or actual damages, whichever is greater, for negligent violations; $5,000 or actual damages for intentional or reckless violations; plus reasonable attorneys' fees and costs and injunctive or other appropriate equitable relief.

first_instance.law_name: Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act, 740 ILCS 14/20

instances.notes: First statutory damages + no-actual-harm-required private right of action for biometric privacy in the world; enabled the landmark $650M Facebook settlement.
Allows individuals to sue for material and non-material damage but requires proof of actual harm; no statutory per-violation amount.
Limited private right of action for data breaches only ($100–$750 statutory damages); no broader PRA for biometric-specific violations.
EU AI Act relies on government-only regulatory fines; no private right of action for individuals.
Enforcement is exclusively by the Colorado Attorney General; no private right of action.

Both create private rights of action with injunctive relief, damages, and attorney's fees for statutory violations, but this rule applies to AI-generated political content violations rather than biometric privacy violations.

Both provide civil remedies including damages for unauthorized use of an individual's biometric or identity-related data, but Georgia's rule covers AI-generated replicas broadly (injunctive relief, actual damages, disgorgement, attorney's fees) while Illinois BIPA is specific to biometric data with statutory per-violation damages.

Both rules establish civil penalty enforcement mechanisms for violations, but this rule sets $5,000 per violation collectible by the AG or local prosecutors, while BIPA creates a private right of action with $1,000–$5,000 per violation.

Both provide statutory damages per violation as an alternative to actual damages, but Arkansas sets a minimum of $10,000 per violation for AI likeness rights while Illinois BIPA sets $1,000–$5,000 for biometric privacy violations.

Both create a private right of action for individuals to sue for violations and recover statutory damages, but this rule is specific to companion chatbot violations rather than biometric privacy, and the damage amounts and structure likely differ.

Both create private rights of action for individuals to sue for actual damages, injunctive relief, and attorney's fees; BIPA applies to biometric privacy violations while the Tennessee rule applies specifically to healthcare AI chatbot violations.

rule_text: Individuals have the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing — including profiling — that produces a legal or similarly significant effect on them, unless they have given explicit consent or it is necessary for a contract.
rule_text_technical: Data subjects shall have the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning them or similarly significantly affects them, except where the processing is necessary for a contract, authorised by Union or Member State law, or based on the data subject's explicit consent.

first_instance.law_name: General Data Protection Regulation, Art. 22

instances.notes: First binding right not to be subject to solely automated consequential decisions; concept traces to France's 1978 Loi Informatique et Libertés.
High-risk AI systems must enable effective human oversight and intervention; functionally implements Art. 22 at the product level.
Individuals may request that a consequential decision made by high-risk AI be reviewed by a human; limited to 'high-risk AI' contexts.
Right to request review of automated decisions that significantly affect individual rights.
Requires notice when AI is used in employment decisions but does not grant a right to human review.
China's framework does not recognize a right against automated consequential decisions; state decisions are expressly permitted.

Both provide users with rights to opt out of or control algorithmic/automated processing, but this rule is specific to algorithmic recommendation services and provides an option to turn off personalization entirely, whereas GDPR Art. 22 focuses on solely automated decisions with legal effects.

Both recognize individuals' rights regarding automated decisions affecting them, but this rule specifically grants a right to understand specific credit denial reasons under ECOA in the US context, while GDPR Art. 22 provides a broader right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with significant effects.

Both rules give individuals rights regarding AI-based decisions affecting them and the right to human review, but this Ontario rule applies to public sector AI use specifically with a right to obtain information and request human review, while GDPR Art. 22 broadly prohibits solely automated decisions with significant effects and provides opt-out rights.

Both address transparency around AI decision-making rationale, but the Kentucky rule creates a government reporting obligation upon request within an agency governance framework, while the GDPR rule grants individuals a right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with broader individual rights.

Both address transparency obligations for automated processing, but Qatar's rule is a general transparency obligation while GDPR Art. 22 specifically addresses the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal effects.
Serbia's Art. 38(1) is a near-verbatim transposition of GDPR Art. 22(1) — the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions including profiling with significant effects.

Both require meaningful explanation of automated decisions to affected individuals, but the Canadian directive is a voluntary policy framework for government departments while GDPR Art. 22 is a binding right with opt-out provisions.

instances.citation: Art. (Automated Decision-Making — Right Not to Be Subject)
instances.notes: Both establish the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing including profiling that produce legal or similarly significant effects, using substantially the same standard.

Both require transparency about automated processing, but the DIFC rule specifically focuses on 'meaningful information' about autonomous/semi-autonomous systems and is more detailed in scope than GDPR Art. 22's general right not to be subject to solely automated decisions.

instances.citation: PDPL Art. (Data Subject Rights) – Right to Object
instances.notes: Both establish a right to object to processing based on legitimate interests and to processing for direct marketing, but PDPL frames this as a data subject right while GDPR Article 22 focuses on automated decisions.

instances.citation: Client Rights in Relation to Automated Recommendations § 1 (Right to Explanation)
instances.notes: Both provide a right to explanation for automated decisions, but this rule is specific to robo-advisory financial recommendations in Mauritius and is from a voluntary instrument, while GDPR Art 22 is a binding right against solely automated decisions.

Both grant individuals the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with significant legal or similarly significant effects; the UAE rule adopts the same substantive standard as GDPR Article 22.

instances.citation: Art. (Rights in Relation to Automated Decisions)
instances.notes: Both establish the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with significant effects and to request human review, consistent with GDPR Article 22.

instances.citation: UU PDP Art. (Right Against Automated Decision-Making)
instances.notes: Both grant individuals the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing including profiling that produces significant effects on them.

Both provide individuals with rights regarding AI-assisted decisions, but Shenzhen's rule is limited to government public service decisions and provides a right to seek explanations rather than a general right not to be subject to solely automated decisions.

Both address explainability of automated decisions affecting individuals, but the GDPR provision is binding and includes a right not to be subject to solely automated decisions, while the ASEAN guide is a voluntary recommendation focused broadly on AI decision explainability.

instances.citation: NDPA 2023, Rights in Relation to Automated Decision-Making
instances.notes: Both establish the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions — including profiling — that produce significant legal or similarly significant effects.

Both address individuals' rights regarding automated decisions; GDPR provides a binding right not to be subject to solely automated decisions while Tunisia recommends protecting digital rights including the right to explanation and human review voluntarily.

Both require informing affected persons of AI use and providing meaningful recourse, but Peru's rule is for deployers generally while the GDPR focuses specifically on solely automated decisions and the right not to be subject to them.

instances.citation: § Rights of Data Subjects — Right Against Automated Decisions
instances.notes: Both grant individuals the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with significant legal or similar effects, with safeguards including human review, consistent with GDPR Art. 22.
Both rules grant individuals the right to receive explanations of AI-assisted decisions that affect them and to contest such decisions, covering the same substantive right.
Both address explainability of AI-influenced decisions to affected individuals, but the GDPR is binding and specific to automated processing while this is a broad voluntary explainability principle.

instances.citation: Ch. 501, Part V, F.S. — Profiling and Automated Decision-Making (Opt-Out)
instances.notes: Both address automated decision-making/profiling rights, but Florida provides an opt-out mechanism while GDPR provides a default right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with limited exceptions.
Both grant individuals the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions that produce significant effects, and the right to human review.
Both rules require notification to individuals when automated decision-making produces legal or similarly significant effects, consistent with GDPR Article 22 obligations.

Both require transparency about automated decision-making, but the Australian rule is a privacy policy disclosure obligation whereas GDPR Art.22 grants a right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal effects.

instances.citation: Art. 21 (Automated Decision-Making – Prohibition on Solely Automated Decisions)
instances.notes: Both prohibit subjecting data subjects to decisions based solely on automated processing including profiling that produce significant effects, with exceptions for consent, contract, or legal authorization.

Both provide affected persons with the right to seek explanations of AI-assisted decisions, but the GDPR is a binding right not to be subject to solely automated decisions while Argentina's rule is a voluntary recommendation for accessible explanation channels in public administration.

instances.citation: LFPDPPP 2025, Automated Decision-Making Chapter — Right to Not Be Subject to Solely Automated Decisions
instances.notes: Both establish the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with significant effects, but Mexico's version is binding domestic law while the GDPR is EU law, and the Mexican rule applies to decisions with 'legal or similarly significant effects' in similar phrasing.

Both address automated decision-making protections, but this rule specifically defines 'based solely on automated processing' by requiring meaningful human involvement, whereas GDPR Art.22 sets out the general right not to be subject to solely automated decisions without defining 'meaningful human involvement'.

Both provide individuals with the right to explanations of AI-assisted decisions; Peru's rule creates a mechanism for affected persons to request explanations in high-risk use cases as a deployer obligation, while GDPR Art. 22 provides a right not to be subject to solely automated decisions.
Both grant individuals the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions producing significant legal or similarly significant effects.
Both require informing individuals when automated decision-making is used and explaining the logic involved; Thailand's rule is framed as a notification duty under the PDPA specific to AI.
Both grant individuals the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing of personal data with significant legal or similarly significant effects.
Both prohibit or restrict automated decision-making that significantly affects data subjects without appropriate safeguards, though Kenya's rule is drafted more briefly.

rule_text: Before deploying any AI system that poses high risks to individuals' rights, the operator must first complete a Data Protection Impact Assessment documenting the risks and mitigation measures.
rule_text_technical: Where a type of processing using new technologies and taking into account the nature, scope, context and purposes of the processing is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller shall carry out an assessment of the impact of the envisaged processing operations on the protection of personal data prior to the processing.

first_instance.law_name: General Data Protection Regulation, Art. 35

instances.notes: First binding pre-deployment impact assessment requirement for high-risk data processing; AI systems using personal data trigger this requirement.
High-risk AI deployers in public contexts must conduct a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment; explicitly builds on GDPR Art. 35.
Requires an algorithmic impact assessment (AIA) for high-risk AI; must cover bias, civil rights impacts, and data governance.
Requires annual independent bias audit of automated employment decision tools, published publicly; narrower than DPIA.
High-risk AI systems must undergo an impact assessment covering societal and individual rights risks before deployment.
CPRA regulations require risk assessments for AI using personal data that presents significant privacy risks.
Generative AI services must undergo a security assessment filed with Chinese regulators before public release.

instances.citation: Part V, Principle 3 – Right to Privacy and Data Protection
instances.notes: Both address protecting privacy throughout the AI lifecycle and establishing data protection frameworks, but UNESCO's rule is a broad voluntary recommendation while GDPR Art. 35 is a binding requirement for Data Protection Impact Assessments on high-risk systems.

Both require a formal data protection impact assessment/management programme before or during processing, but Sri Lanka's rule also requires catalogued compliance records and a broader Data Protection Management Programme, going beyond GDPR's DPIA scope.

Both require a comprehensive impact/risk assessment before deployment, but the GDPR Art. 35 is binding and focuses on data protection impact, while this voluntary Canadian rule covers broader adverse impacts including rights, safety, and fairness for generative AI.

Both require impact assessments addressing AI-related risks including ethical considerations, but GDPR Art. 35 is a binding requirement specifically for data protection impact assessments for high-risk processing, while ISO 42001 is a voluntary, broader AI impact assessment recommendation.

Both rules connect AI system oversight with data protection supervision, but this rule specifically designates Datatilsynet as the competent authority for EU AI Act supervision where personal data processing is involved, which is a national implementation detail beyond GDPR's DPIA requirement.

Both require action before deployment of high-risk AI systems — Vietnam mandates remediation and incident reporting after a serious incident, while the GDPR requires a Data Protection Impact Assessment before deployment; the operational obligations differ significantly.
Serbia's DPIA provision is a near-verbatim transposition of GDPR Art. 35 — requiring a Data Protection Impact Assessment before high-risk processing.

Both require a pre-deployment impact assessment for AI/automated decision systems, but the Canadian directive requires public publication of results and is a voluntary policy framework, while GDPR Art. 35 is a binding DPIA requirement with different procedural specifics.

Both require a Data Protection Impact Assessment before deploying high-risk automated/AI systems, with substantively the same requirement though the DIFC rule specifically references autonomous and semi-autonomous systems.
Both require a data protection impact assessment before high-risk processing operations; the UAE rule mirrors the GDPR DPIA obligation but is issued under UAE law.
Both require a Data Protection Impact Assessment before commencing high-risk processing activities; Rwanda's version is functionally equivalent to GDPR Article 35.

instances.citation: UU PDP Art. (Data Protection Impact Assessment — DPIA)
instances.notes: Both require a Data Protection Impact Assessment before commencing high-risk processing activities likely to result in significant risks to data subjects' rights.
Both require security/risk assessments before deploying AI systems, but this rule is specific to deep synthesis tools and allows self-assessment or third-party professional body assessment.

Both require risk assessments prior to deploying AI systems, but the GDPR provision is a binding Data Protection Impact Assessment requirement for high-risk processing, while the ASEAN guide is a voluntary recommendation covering broader risk identification including failure modes.

Both require a Data Protection Impact Assessment before processing that poses high risks to individuals' rights, with NDPA adding consultation with the NDPC where high residual risk cannot be mitigated.

Both require pre-deployment review for AI systems that may materially impact individuals' rights and dignity, but this rule mandates a broader ethics review process in China's S&T framework, while GDPR requires a Data Protection Impact Assessment focused on data privacy risks.

Both address impact assessment for AI systems affecting individuals; GDPR mandates Data Protection Impact Assessments for high-risk processing as a binding requirement while Tunisia recommends promoting algorithmic impact assessment practices voluntarily.

Both require risk assessments before deploying AI systems, but Peru's rule applies proportionately to all AI systems before market placement, while the GDPR specifically requires a Data Protection Impact Assessment for high-risk processing.
Both require a Data Protection Impact Assessment before commencing high-risk processing activities including large-scale sensitive data processing, consistent with GDPR Art. 35.

Both rules require pre-deployment impact assessments for AI in high-stakes contexts, but Guangdong's rule is specifically framed as an 'algorithmic impact assessment' rather than a data protection impact assessment.

instances.citation: Section IV, Human Rights Impact Assessments
instances.notes: Both require impact assessments before deploying AI in sensitive contexts, but the GDPR requires a binding Data Protection Impact Assessment while this voluntary rule calls for human rights impact assessments more broadly.
Both require a Data Protection Impact Assessment before commencing high-risk processing activities.

Both rules require a privacy/data protection impact assessment before deploying AI systems that make automated decisions with significant effects on individuals, matching the GDPR DPIA obligation for high-risk processing.
Both require a security/risk assessment before deploying high-risk AI/biometric systems, but this rule is specific to facial recognition technology products and services in China.
Both require conducting a Data Protection Impact Assessment before undertaking high-risk processing likely to result in significant risks to individuals' rights, matching the DPIA obligation.

Both require impact assessments before deploying AI in high-stakes contexts, but the GDPR mandates a formal DPIA as a binding requirement while this Argentine rule is a voluntary recommendation for AI systems affecting rights.

instances.citation: LFPDPPP 2025, Automated Decision-Making Chapter — Algorithmic Impact Assessment
instances.notes: Both require impact assessments before high-risk automated processing, but Mexico's rule is specifically framed as an 'Algorithmic Impact Assessment' with triggers related to scale, sensitive data, or profiling, while GDPR Art. 35 is a broader DPIA requirement.

Both require a pre-deployment conformity/impact assessment for high-risk AI systems; Peru calls it a 'conformity assessment' under SNGD guidelines while GDPR calls it a DPIA, and the scope and procedural details differ.
Both require a Data Protection Impact Assessment before commencing high-risk processing activities, reflecting the same substantive obligation.
Both require a Data Protection Impact Assessment before deploying AI systems that pose high risk to individuals' rights; Thailand's DPIA requirement closely mirrors GDPR Article 35.
Both require a data protection impact assessment before undertaking processing activities likely to result in high risk to individuals' rights, with the same substantive trigger and obligation.

rule_text: Individuals have the right to request deletion of their personal data, and this right extends to data used to train AI systems.
rule_text_technical: The data subject shall have the right to obtain from the controller the erasure of personal data concerning him or her without undue delay where the personal data are no longer necessary in relation to the purposes for which they were collected or processed, or the data subject withdraws consent.

first_instance.law_name: General Data Protection Regulation, Art. 17

instances.notes: First codified 'right to be forgotten' as a binding legal entitlement; enforced against AI training datasets by DPAs since 2023.
Provides a consumer right to deletion of personal information; applies to data held by AI developers and deployers.
Right to anonymization, blocking, or elimination of unnecessary or unlawful data; similar scope to GDPR Art. 17.
Right to correct data used in high-risk AI decisions but no standalone deletion right.

Both require deletion/erasure of personal data when the purpose for processing no longer exists, with similar scope covering controller-initiated and data-subject-requested erasure; independently drafted but substantively equivalent.

Both grant individuals the right to request correction/deletion of inaccurate or incomplete personal data, but Sri Lanka's rule focuses on rectification and completion while GDPR's Article 17 focuses on erasure/right to be forgotten.

Both require providers to respond to individuals' requests to access, correct, or delete their personal data, independently adopted in Chinese and EU law though with different specific rights enumerated.

instances.citation: Art. 6 / Rights of Data Owners — Right to Deletion
instances.notes: Both grant individuals the right to request deletion of personal data that is no longer necessary for its original purpose; Colombia's formulation is consistent with GDPR's right to erasure but drafted independently.

instances.citation: Rights of Data Subjects – Right to Erasure
instances.notes: Both provide a right to erasure/deletion when data is no longer necessary for the original purpose, independently drafted.
Serbia's right to erasure is a near-verbatim transposition of GDPR Art. 17 — covering the same grounds for deletion including lack of necessity, consent withdrawal, and unlawful processing.
Both establish the right to erasure/deletion where data is no longer necessary, consent has been withdrawn, or other specified grounds apply, with similar enumerated conditions.

instances.citation: PDPL Art. (Data Subject Rights) – Right to Erasure
instances.notes: Both establish a right to erasure/deletion of personal data when it is no longer necessary for the original purpose or when consent is withdrawn.
Both grant individuals the right to request deletion of personal data where it is no longer necessary or consent is withdrawn; the UAE rule independently adopts the same substantive standard.
Both establish the right to erasure where data is no longer necessary, consent is withdrawn, or processing is unlawful, consistent with GDPR Article 17.
Both provide individuals the right to erasure of their personal data where it is no longer needed, consent is withdrawn, or other specified conditions are met.
Both establish a right to erasure of personal data where no longer necessary, consent is withdrawn, or other specified grounds are met.

instances.citation: § Rights of Data Subjects — Right to Erasure
instances.notes: Both grant individuals the right to erasure of personal data where it is no longer necessary or where consent is withdrawn, consistent with the GDPR right to be forgotten.

instances.citation: Ch. 501, Part V, F.S. — Consumer Rights (Right to Delete)
instances.notes: Both establish a right to deletion of personal data; Florida's version is limited to data the consumer provided or that was obtained about them, while GDPR's extends explicitly to AI training data.
Both grant individuals the right to erasure/deletion of personal data where it is no longer necessary or consent has been withdrawn.

Both rules establish a right to erasure and specify grounds including unlawful processing and data no longer being necessary, but the Israeli rule adds a specific 30-day compliance deadline not explicit in the GDPR rule and extends it to AI training data.

Both grant individuals the right to erasure of personal data where it is no longer necessary for the original purpose or other grounds apply, though Chile's rule may not extend explicitly to AI training data as the GDPR rule does.
Both grant individuals the right to erasure of personal data where it is no longer necessary or consent is withdrawn.

Both address consumers' right to delete personal information, but this rule is specific to data broker websites and requires a webpage explanation of the deletion process, whereas the GDPR rule addresses the right to erasure more broadly.

Both recognise a bundle of data subject rights including access, correction, and deletion, but Kenya's rule enumerates these rights together in a single provision whereas the GDPR separates them across multiple articles.

Both require erasure of data when no longer needed, but the Data Act applies to third-party recipients of IoT/product data upon purpose completion rather than to personal data erasure on individual request.

rule_text: Consumers have the right to opt out of the sale or sharing of their personal data, including data used to train AI systems or for targeted advertising.
rule_text_technical: A consumer shall have the right, at any time, to direct a business that sells personal information about the consumer to third parties not to sell the consumer's personal information (opt-out right). Amended by CPRA to also cover sharing of personal information for cross-context behavioral advertising.

first_instance.law_name: California Consumer Privacy Act / CPRA, § 1798.120

instances.notes: First US law granting a general opt-out right against data sale and sharing; extended by CPRA to cover sharing for behavioral advertising.
Right to object to processing for direct marketing (absolute) and other purposes (qualified); opt-out rather than opt-in for most processing.
Right to object to processing based on legitimate interest or public interest, but no explicit opt-out from data sale.

Both give individuals the right to withdraw/opt out of data processing and require a convenient mechanism; PIPL frames this as consent withdrawal with a binding effect on further processing, while CCPA focuses on opt-out of sale/sharing; scope and mechanism differ meaningfully.

Both give users rights to control how their data/tags are used in algorithmic systems, but this rule specifically requires providers to offer functions to select or delete user tags in recommendation services, while CCPA focuses on opt-out of sale/sharing of personal data.

Both rules restrict the collection, sale, or sharing of consumer personal data, but Maryland's rule is narrowly focused on prohibiting such practices specifically for the purpose of determining or adjusting grocery/essential goods prices, while CCPA provides a broader opt-out right for data sale/sharing across all purposes.

Serbia's right to object covers processing based on legitimate interests and direct marketing, mirroring GDPR Art. 21, whereas CCPA's opt-out focuses specifically on sale/sharing of data — similar concept but different scope.

instances.citation: Ch. 501, Part V, F.S. — Consumer Rights (Right to Opt-Out of Sale/Targeted Advertising)
instances.notes: Both grant the right to opt out of sale and targeted advertising using personal data; Florida's version is independently drafted but substantively equivalent.

Both address consumers' right to opt out of the sale or sharing of personal data, but this rule requires data brokers to publish a specific webpage explaining the opt-out process, while the CCPA rule broadly establishes the right itself.
Both grant the right to opt out of certain uses of personal data for marketing; CCPA covers sale/sharing broadly while POPIA focuses specifically on electronic direct marketing opt-out.

rule_text: Employers using automated tools to screen or rank job candidates must notify candidates before the interview that such a tool is being used, and must publish an annual independent bias audit of the tool.
rule_text_technical: It shall be unlawful for an employer or employment agency to use an automated employment decision tool (AEDT) to screen a candidate or employee in the city of New York unless: (1) the tool has been the subject of a bias audit conducted no more than one year prior; (2) a summary of the results of the most recent bias audit has been made publicly available; (3) the employer has notified candidates of the use of such tool.

first_instance.law_name: New York City Local Law 144, § 20-871

instances.notes: First binding annual-audit + public-disclosure requirement for AI hiring tools; used 'bias audit' framing that influenced subsequent state laws.
Employment AI is classified as high-risk; requires conformity assessment and documentation before deployment, but no mandatory annual external audit.
High-risk AI in employment requires algorithmic impact assessment and candidate notice, but assessment is internal rather than independent.
Prohibits AI-driven employment discrimination in Illinois; strict liability for disparate impact — stronger substantive standard than NYC LL 144's transparency-only approach.

Both require advance notice to individuals that an automated decision system will be used, but the Canadian directive applies to government service delivery across all channels rather than employment screening specifically.

rule_text: AI systems that evaluate or classify people based on their social behaviour or personal characteristics in order to assign a social score used to restrict or harm them are absolutely prohibited.
rule_text_technical: The placing on the market, putting into service and use of AI systems that evaluate or classify natural persons or groups of persons over a certain period of time based on their social behaviour or known, inferred or predicted personal or personality characteristics, with the social score leading to either detrimental or unfavourable treatment of those persons or groups in social contexts unrelated to the contexts in which the data was originally generated, shall be prohibited.

first_instance.law_name: EU AI Act, Art. 5(1)(c)

instances.notes: First binding prohibition on AI social scoring systems in any major jurisdiction.
TRAIGA prohibits AI systems that create or implement social credit scores affecting individual rights or opportunities.
China's framework permits and deploys social credit and social scoring as a state governance mechanism — the exact practice the EU prohibition targets.
Brazil prohibits AI systems used for social scoring resulting in discriminatory harm, but framing focuses on discrimination rather than the categorical EU ban.

instances.citation: Part V, Principle 1 – Proportionality and Do No Harm
instances.notes: Both address prohibiting AI-based discrimination, mass surveillance, and psychological manipulation, but the UNESCO rule is a voluntary recommendation while the EU AI Act binding prohibition is more specific to social scoring.

Both prohibit AI-based social scoring systems that evaluate or classify people based on social behaviour or personal characteristics; Kazakhstan's formulation is functionally identical in substance to the EU AI Act's Article 5(1)(c) prohibition.

Both require AI to be fair, non-discriminatory, and non-harmful, but Vietnam's rule is broader and also adds transparency, no harm to humans or society, and safety as affirmative requirements, while the EU AI Act rule specifically prohibits social scoring systems.

Both address AI systems used for social monitoring, tracking, and profiling, but this rule mandates a pre-use ethics review in China's S&T framework, while the EU AI Act prohibits such systems outright when used to assign social scores.
Both prohibit AI systems used by public authorities for social scoring of the general population based on social behavior or personal characteristics.

Both prohibit AI systems used to classify or profile individuals based on biometric data for discriminatory purposes related to race, religion, etc., but the Chinese rule is specific to facial recognition technology.

Both address AI-generated discrimination based on protected characteristics, but the EU AI Act prohibits social scoring systems specifically while this Argentine rule is a broader voluntary recommendation against discrimination.

instances.citation: LFPDPPP 2025, Automated Decision-Making Chapter — Prohibition on Discriminatory Automated Processing
instances.notes: The EU AI Act prohibits AI-based social scoring systems, while Mexico's rule prohibits discriminatory automated processing based on protected characteristics; both address discriminatory automated processing but the EU rule is broader and targets social scoring specifically.

Both prohibit discriminatory AI content practices, but this rule specifically prohibits discriminatory content moderation by network operators while the EU rule prohibits social scoring systems — different context and mechanism.

rule_text: AI systems that use subliminal techniques, deceptive tactics, or psychological manipulation to influence people's decisions in ways that harm them are absolutely prohibited.
rule_text_technical: The placing on the market, putting into service and use of AI systems that deploy subliminal techniques beyond a person's consciousness or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques, with the objective or the effect of materially distorting the behaviour of a person or a group of persons by appreciably impairing their ability to make an informed decision, thereby causing them to take a decision they would not have otherwise taken in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause that person significant harm, shall be prohibited.

first_instance.law_name: EU AI Act, Art. 5(1)(a)

instances.notes: First binding prohibition on AI-powered subliminal manipulation techniques in any major jurisdiction.
Prohibits AI systems designed to manipulate individuals through psychological mechanisms that impair free decision-making.
Prohibits AI designed to manipulate an individual through psychological exploitation; requires intentional design element.

instances.citation: Part V, Principle 1 – Proportionality and Do No Harm
instances.notes: Both address proportionality and limiting AI use to legitimate aims without causing harm, but the UNESCO rule is a voluntary broad principle while the EU AI Act binding rule specifically prohibits subliminal and manipulative techniques.

Both prohibit using AI/algorithms to harm public order or manipulate users, but this rule is broader in scope (national security, economic order, social order) and specific to algorithmic recommendation services, while the EU AI Act focuses on subliminal manipulation.

Both require measures to prevent discriminatory or harmful AI outputs, but the Chinese rule specifically addresses algorithm design and training data selection to prevent discrimination, while the EU rule prohibits subliminal manipulation techniques.

Both prohibit deceptive AI content targeting individuals' decisions, but the Indiana rule is narrowly scoped to political advertisements containing synthetic media of real candidates near elections, whereas the EU AI Act broadly prohibits subliminal/deceptive AI manipulation across all contexts.

Both protect human dignity and individual autonomy against harmful AI, but the Convention imposes a positive State obligation to adopt measures respecting dignity and autonomy across the full AI lifecycle, while the EU AI Act prohibits specific manipulative techniques by operators.

Both address maximum penalties for prohibited AI practices under the EU AI Act (€35M or 7% of turnover), but the existing rule addresses the substantive prohibition while the Hungarian rule addresses the domestic penalty implementation for those violations.

Both prohibit AI systems that use manipulative or subliminal techniques to distort users' decision-making; Kazakhstan's phrasing targets subconscious influence while the EU AI Act references subliminal techniques and psychological manipulation, but the substantive standard is the same.

Both prohibit using AI to deceive or manipulate perception; Vietnam's rule is broader, also explicitly prohibiting harmful deepfakes, IP infringement, and illegal data processing, going beyond the EU AI Act's subliminal/psychological manipulation focus.

Both prohibit AI from using psychological manipulation, but this rule is specifically targeted at AI companion chatbots generating outputs promoting isolation from family or friends for minor users, a narrower and more specific application.

instances.citation: Fiduciary Duties and Conduct Standards § 2 (Prohibition on Misleading Conduct)
instances.notes: Both prohibit misleading or deceptive conduct involving AI systems, but this rule is specific to robo-advisory algorithm design and client disclosures in financial services, while the EU AI Act's Art 5a focuses on subliminal manipulation broadly.

Both prohibit using AI to manipulate individuals or engage in deceptive practices, but the EU AI Act is binding and specifically prohibits subliminal and psychological manipulation techniques, while the ASEAN guide is a voluntary recommendation against circumventing legal obligations and deceptive use.

Both address AI systems that generate or manipulate content in ways that may mislead users, but this rule mandates a pre-use ethics review in China's S&T framework, while the EU AI Act prohibits subliminal manipulation techniques outright.
Both address safety and harm prevention in AI design, but Peru's rule is a general safety design principle while the EU AI Act specifically prohibits subliminal/deceptive manipulation techniques.

Both prohibit AI systems using manipulative techniques that exploit consumer psychology; the EU AI Act focuses on subliminal/deceptive techniques while this FTC rule focuses on AI-personalized dark patterns.

Both prohibit deceptive AI designs that mislead users, but Florida's rule is specifically targeted at chatbots deceiving consumers into believing they are communicating with a human, while the EU AI Act's prohibition is broader covering subliminal and psychological manipulation.

Both prohibit AI-generated content designed to deceive audiences, but this rule focuses specifically on deceptive AI-generated content distribution by platforms, while the EU rule broadly prohibits subliminal and manipulative AI techniques.

Both prohibit AI systems used for harmful/malicious purposes, but this rule specifically prohibits offensive cyberattack tools while the EU AI Act prohibits manipulation and subliminal techniques — different scope and domain.
Both rules prohibit coercion, deception, or manipulation, but the AI Act targets AI systems influencing decisions while the Data Act targets data access contexts specifically.

rule_text: Real-time remote biometric identification of individuals in publicly accessible spaces by law enforcement AI is prohibited, except under narrow judicial-authorised exceptions for specific serious crimes.
rule_text_technical: The use by or on behalf of competent authorities of 'real-time' remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for the purpose of law enforcement shall be prohibited unless strictly necessary for limited objectives, including the search for missing victims, prevention of specific terrorist threats, or prosecution of criminals for serious offences listed in Annex II, and subject to prior judicial authorisation.

first_instance.law_name: EU AI Act, Art. 5(1)(h)

instances.notes: First binding prohibition on real-time public biometric surveillance by law enforcement in any major jurisdiction.
Consent-first rule effectively prohibits mass public biometric collection, but applies to private entities only, not law enforcement.
China operates one of the world's largest public biometric surveillance systems; no prohibition on real-time identification.

Both address biometric data use in AI systems including facial recognition, but this rule requires a mandatory ethics review before use, while the EU AI Act imposes an outright prohibition on real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces by law enforcement.
Both prohibit real-time remote biometric identification of persons in publicly accessible spaces, with Peru's rule mirroring the EU AI Act's general prohibition.

Both restrict covert biometric identification via AI; the EU AI Act prohibits real-time remote biometric ID by law enforcement in public spaces while this FTC rule broadly prohibits covert biometric tracking in commercial consumer contexts.

Both address AI surveillance compliance with legal standards, but the EU AI Act binding prohibition targets specific real-time biometric ID by law enforcement while this voluntary rule broadly addresses AI-assisted surveillance compliance with international human rights law.

Both address biometric identification AI as high-risk/prohibited, but Peru classifies real-time and post-hoc biometric identification broadly as high-risk rather than prohibiting real-time remote biometric ID by law enforcement specifically as the EU AI Act does.

rule_text: High-risk AI systems must be designed so that humans can effectively oversee, monitor, and intervene or override the system's outputs. Oversight must be more than nominal.
rule_text_technical: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which the AI system is in use. Providers shall ensure that operators can intervene, override, or stop the system.

first_instance.law_name: EU AI Act, Art. 14

instances.notes: First product-level design requirement for meaningful human oversight of high-risk AI systems.
GDPR requires that automated decisions under Art. 22 must allow human intervention and contest; AI Act operationalises this at the system design level.
High-risk AI deployers must provide a mechanism for consumers to appeal or review AI decisions; does not specify design requirements.
High-risk AI must include human oversight mechanisms and allow operators to override or stop outputs.

Both require oversight and monitoring of AI systems, but this rule specifically mandates periodic auditing of algorithm mechanisms and prohibits configuring algorithms to induce addiction or excessive use, which is more specific than the EU AI Act's human oversight requirement.

Both require transparency and reliability measures in AI systems, but the Chinese rule focuses on accuracy and reliability of generated content while the EU rule focuses on human oversight and intervention capabilities for high-risk systems.

instances.citation: Proposed Rule 15l-2 / Advisers Act Rule — Core Requirement 3(d)
instances.notes: Both require ongoing monitoring of AI systems, but the EU AI Act focuses on human oversight of high-risk AI generally, while this SEC rule specifically requires ongoing monitoring of covered technologies for new or changed conflicts of interest in financial services.

instances.citation: Measures Table — Human Oversight and Monitoring, Row 1
instances.notes: Both require human oversight and monitoring of AI system operation, but the EU AI Act is binding and applies specifically to high-risk AI with intervention and override capabilities, while this voluntary Canadian rule more broadly recommends operational monitoring of generative AI.

Both address compliance with AI regulations in controlled sandbox environments, but this rule specifically concerns sandbox participation and compliance with EU/national rules (including GDPR and AI Act), whereas the existing rule focuses on human oversight of high-risk AI systems.

Both require transparency and human oversight of AI systems, but the Convention sets a general State obligation to ensure adequate and context-specific transparency and oversight across the lifecycle, while the EU AI Act prescribes detailed technical human oversight requirements for high-risk systems specifically.

Both rules require transparency about AI use and an accountability framework with human oversight, but this Ontario rule applies specifically to public sector institutions and is a binding statute, whereas the EU AI Act's Art. 14 focuses on high-risk AI system design requirements for operators more broadly, with different scope and specific obligations.

Both address human oversight and prohibition on delegating critical decisions to AI, but Nevada's rule is sector-specific to licensed mental health professionals and focuses on clinical judgment and therapeutic treatment decisions rather than general high-risk AI oversight.

Both relate to high-risk AI system obligations under the EU AI Act; the existing rule addresses the substantive human oversight requirement while the Hungarian rule establishes the domestic penalty tier (€15M or 3% of turnover) for violations of those obligations.

Both require that AI systems serve humans without replacing human authority and responsibility, and mandate human oversight and intervention capability, though Vietnam's formulation is broader and less technically detailed.

Both rules restrict sole reliance on automated/AI processes for consequential decisions (downcoding here vs. high-risk AI oversight generally), but this Indiana rule is narrowly sector-specific to health benefits claim downcoding while the EU AI Act art.14 is a broad human oversight requirement for high-risk AI systems.

EU AI Act Art. 14 requires human oversight over high-risk AI systems; the Tennessee rule specifically mandates that a licensed professional review and take responsibility for any diagnosis, prescription, or treatment recommendation generated by AI in clinical settings.

Both require ongoing monitoring of AI/automated decision system outcomes to detect unintended bias or errors, but the Canadian directive is a voluntary government policy while the EU AI Act Art. 14 is a binding requirement for high-risk AI systems.

Both recommend human oversight and intervention mechanisms for AI, but the EU AI Act is a binding requirement specific to high-risk AI systems while the OECD principle is a voluntary recommendation applicable broadly.

Both require ongoing monitoring and oversight of automated/AI systems, but the DIFC rule frames this as a data protection obligation with periodic auditing requirements, while the EU AI Act focuses on human oversight design for high-risk AI systems.

instances.citation: PDPL Art. (Automated Decision-Making) – Human Review Requirement
instances.notes: Both require that a qualified human with appropriate authority can review and override automated decisions affecting individuals.

Both require designated human accountability over AI system outputs, but this rule is specific to financial advisory services and requires a named senior compliance/technology officer, while the EU AI Act sets a broader high-risk AI human oversight standard.
Both address defining roles for human oversight in AI systems, but EU AI Act is binding and focused on high-risk systems while NIST RMF is voluntary and broader in scope.

Both require the ability to override, correct, or shut down AI systems through human oversight mechanisms, but the EU AI Act is binding and applies to high-risk AI systems specifically, while the ASEAN guide is a voluntary broader recommendation.

Both address AI systems with autonomous decision-making deployed in physical environments, but this rule mandates a pre-deployment ethics review in China's S&T framework, while the EU AI Act requires human oversight mechanisms for high-risk AI systems.

Both address transparency and explainability requirements for high-stakes AI systems; the EU AI Act mandates human oversight for high-risk AI systems as a binding requirement while Tunisia recommends establishing transparency and explainability requirements voluntarily.

Both address reliability, robustness, and resilience of AI systems, but Peru's rule is a general design principle while the EU AI Act's Art. 14 specifically focuses on human oversight mechanisms for high-risk systems.
Both rules require human oversight mechanisms for AI-assisted decisions that significantly affect individuals' rights and interests, though framed differently.
Both require human oversight and accountability for AI systems, but the EU AI Act is binding and specific to high-risk systems while this voluntary principle applies broadly to all AI.

Both address human oversight over AI decisions affecting individuals, but the EU AI Act is a binding requirement for high-risk AI while this is a voluntary recommendation for significant decisions affecting rights and interests.

Both require human oversight/intervention capability for high-risk AI, but Utah specifically frames this as a consumer right to request human review in defined high-risk interaction categories, whereas the EU AI Act focuses on system design for operator oversight.
Both require high-risk AI systems to be designed so humans can effectively oversee, monitor, and intervene; Peru's rule mirrors this substantive standard as an independent binding obligation.

Both require human oversight mechanisms for AI-assisted decisions in high-stakes contexts, but this rule specifically applies to critical information infrastructure operators while the EU rule applies broadly to high-risk AI systems.
Both require human oversight mechanisms allowing qualified personnel to review and override automated decisions; Thailand's rule applies this through PDPA safeguards rather than a standalone AI Act.

rule_text: Users must be clearly informed when they are interacting with an AI system, not a human. This applies to chatbots, voice assistants, and any AI designed for direct human interaction.
rule_text_technical: Providers of AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons shall ensure that those natural persons are informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the context.

first_instance.law_name: EU AI Act, Art. 50(1)

instances.notes: First major binding chatbot/AI interaction disclosure requirement in a comprehensive AI governance law.
Texas TRAIGA adopts the same disclosure obligation in functionally identical language.
Generative AI services must prominently label AI-generated content and notify users of AI system interactions.
AI systems that interact directly with users must identify themselves as AI.

Both require informing users about automated/AI-driven services, but this rule specifically requires disclosure of algorithmic recommendation service circumstances rather than merely identifying AI vs. human interaction.

Both require mechanisms to inform users they are interacting with AI rather than a human, but the EU AI Act is binding and applies broadly to chatbots and voice assistants, while this voluntary Canadian rule specifically recommends a freely accessible AI content detection tool.

Both rules require public disclosure of information about AI system use, but this Ontario rule targets public sector institutions with prescribed disclosure about AI in decisions, while the EU AI Act Art. 50a focuses on informing users interacting with AI systems such as chatbots across all sectors.

Both require public disclosure of AI use, but the Kentucky rule is limited to government agency contexts with disclosure triggers determined by a governance committee, while the EU AI Act's rule mandates user notification when interacting with AI systems broadly.

Both address AI impersonation of human roles, but Nevada specifically prohibits AI platforms from representing themselves as licensed mental health professionals, which is a narrower, sector-specific prohibition with a higher burden than the EU AI Act's general disclosure requirement.

Both require disclosure when consumers interact with AI rather than a human, but Maine's rule is binding and consumer-transaction-specific while the EU AI Act's Art. 50a is broader in scope and applies to any AI interaction context including chatbots and voice assistants.

Both require disclosure that users are interacting with AI rather than a human, but this rule is specific to companion chatbots and mandates a 'clear and conspicuous' notification format, while the EU AI Act applies broadly to chatbots and voice assistants.

Both require that users be notified when interacting with an AI system rather than a human; Kazakhstan's rule also covers AI-assisted services, which is a minor scope extension but the substantive transparency standard is the same.

Both require disclosure when users interact with AI rather than a human, but this rule is narrower (AI companion chatbots only) and adds a 'clear and conspicuous' standard not specified in the EU AI Act provision.

Both require clear disclosure to users that they are interacting with an AI system, but Idaho's rule is specific to 'conversational AI services' while the EU AI Act applies broadly to chatbots and voice assistants.

EU AI Act Art. 50a requires disclosure that users are interacting with an AI rather than a human; the Tennessee rule adds a specific prohibition on using a human name with professional titles (Dr., R.N., etc.) in healthcare chatbots, making it narrower and more specific in scope.

Both require disclosure when users interact with AI rather than a human, but Oregon's rule is specific to 'artificial output' in a conversational AI context and uses a 'reasonable person' standard, while the EU AI Act broadly covers chatbots and voice assistants with a clearer systemic obligation.

Both address making stakeholders aware of AI interactions, but the EU AI Act is a binding disclosure requirement for chatbots and voice assistants while the OECD principle is a voluntary recommendation including workplace contexts.

Both require informing users they are interacting with an AI system, but this rule is sector-specific to financial advisory services and is a binding regulatory requirement in Mauritius rather than the EU AI Act's broader scope.

Both relate to AI disclosure/labeling obligations for content not covered by mandatory labeling; this rule adds a user-facing labeling function requirement, while the EU AI Act focuses on chatbot/voice assistant disclosure.

Both require informing users when interacting with an AI system, but the EU AI Act is binding and specific to chatbots and voice assistants, while the ASEAN guide is a voluntary broader recommendation.
Both require transparency so users understand they are interacting with AI, but Peru's rule is broader, covering explainability of AI decision-making processes, not just chatbot identity disclosure.
Both require disclosure when consumers interact with AI rather than humans; the EU AI Act provision is binding and broader in scope while this FTC rule focuses specifically on consumer interactions.

Both require disclosure to consumers when they are interacting with an AI system rather than a human; the EU AI Act Art. 50a covers chatbots and voice assistants broadly while this Colorado rule applies to any consumer-facing AI interaction.

Both require clear disclosure at the start of consumer interactions that the user is communicating with an AI/chatbot rather than a human; Florida's version is binding state law covering commercial chatbots.

Both require informing affected persons when AI is used in decisions affecting them, but the EU AI Act mandates disclosure when interacting with AI systems broadly while Argentina's rule is a voluntary recommendation specifically for public administration decisions.

Both require disclosure when AI is used in consumer-facing interactions, but Utah's rule is broader (all generative AI consumer interactions) while EU AI Act focuses on chatbots/voice assistants, and Utah adds a 'clear and conspicuous' standard with specific content requirements.

Both require disclosure when users interact with AI (chatbots, etc.) to avoid deception; Peru frames this as a 'limited-risk' classification obligation while the EU AI Act imposes a direct transparency obligation.

instances.citation: Obligations for Generative AI Service Providers — Disclosure at Point of Creation (¶a)
instances.notes: Both require disclosure when users are interacting with or receiving AI-generated content, but this rule is specifically about disclosure at the point of content creation to the creator-user, whereas the EU rule focuses on informing users they are interacting with an AI system.

rule_text: AI-generated images, audio, and video must be marked with a machine-readable watermark or provenance label so that the content's artificial origin can be detected.
rule_text_technical: Providers of general-purpose AI models shall ensure that AI-generated content is marked in a machine-readable format, and is detectable as artificially generated or manipulated using automated means, through technical solutions such as watermarks, metadata identifications, or cryptographic methods.

first_instance.law_name: EU AI Act, Art. 50(4)

instances.notes: First binding machine-readable watermarking / provenance requirement for AI-generated content.
Requires AI-generated content to be marked with conspicuous labels and to embed machine-readable watermarks.
Requires AI-generated content to include invisible cryptographic watermarks detectable by a free public tool.
Requires platforms to remove non-consensual intimate AI content but does not mandate watermarking at generation.

Both address marking or disclosing AI-generated content, but the EU AI Act is binding and requires machine-readable watermarks, while this voluntary Canadian rule recommends that managers ensure systems interacting with humans identify themselves as AI.

instances.citation: Part I, Principle 7 / Part II, Action 7
instances.notes: Both address content authentication and watermarking/provenance labeling for AI-generated content, but the EU AI Act is a binding requirement while the G7 rule is a voluntary recommendation and also encompasses broader provenance mechanisms beyond watermarking.

Both require disclosure/labeling of AI-generated content, but Indiana mandates a specific human-readable textual disclosure in political advertisements, while the EU AI Act requires machine-readable watermarks or provenance labels for AI-generated images, audio, and video broadly.

Both rules require disclosure/labeling of AI-generated content, but this rule creates a user-opt-in manifest (visible) disclosure obligation for GenAI systems, while the EU AI Act mandates machine-readable watermarks as a blanket requirement.

Both require machine-readable labelling of AI-generated synthetic content (deepfakes, generated images/audio/video); Kazakhstan extends this to a human-readable label requirement as well, but the core substantive standard matches.

Both require marking/labeling of AI-generated audio, images, and video content and notifying users when AI-generated content is present; Vietnam's rule applies to deployers specifically, while the EU AI Act applies to providers with machine-readable watermarks.

Both address technical mechanisms to bolster information integrity and identify AI-generated content, but the EU AI Act mandates machine-readable watermarks for specific content types while OECD frames it as a voluntary feasibility-dependent recommendation.
Both require machine-readable watermarks or provenance labels on AI-generated content; this rule specifies non-intrusive symbols attached to deep synthesis content using technical measures.

Both require marking AI-generated content with identification/watermarks, but this Beijing rule is a binding local regulation applying to text, pictures, audio, and video from generative AI services, while the EU AI Act focuses on machine-readable watermarks for provenance detection.

Both require visible labelling of AI-generated content, but this rule adds specific requirements for standardized wording and prominent display, while the EU rule focuses on machine-readable watermarks and provenance; this is also a binding national standard with more granular display requirements.

instances.citation: Mandatory Labeling Obligations for SSMIs — AI Content Labeling Requirement (¶3)
instances.notes: Both require machine-readable watermarks or provenance mechanisms for AI-generated content, but this rule adds cryptographic signatures and metadata tagging and applies specifically to platform detection obligations, while the EU rule focuses on content providers marking outputs.

rule_text: Providers of general-purpose AI models must comply with EU copyright law when training their models, and must make available a summary of the training data used to allow copyright holders to assess whether their works were included.
rule_text_technical: Providers of general-purpose AI models shall put in place a policy to comply with Union copyright law, and in particular to identify and comply with opt-out reservations expressed pursuant to Article 4(3) of Directive 2019/790 on copyright in the Digital Single Market; and make publicly available a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for training.

first_instance.law_name: EU AI Act, Art. 53(1)(c)–(d)

instances.notes: First binding requirement combining copyright opt-out compliance with public training data summary disclosure for GPAI providers.
Requires AI developers to publish a training data card publicly, but does not address copyright opt-out compliance specifically.
Training data must comply with intellectual property law; no opt-out mechanism or public summary requirement.

Both require disclosure of training data information, but the EU AI Act is binding and focuses on copyright compliance and making training data summaries available, while this voluntary Canadian rule recommends publishing a description of training data types.

instances.citation: Part I, Principle 11 / Part II, Action 11
instances.notes: Both address data input measures and protections for intellectual property and personal data in AI development, but the EU AI Act is a binding rule focused on copyright compliance and transparency summaries for GPAI, while the G7 rule is a broader voluntary recommendation covering both personal data and IP protections.

Both address use of copyrighted works for AI training, but Kazakhstan adopts an opt-out model (use is permitted unless the rights-holder has explicitly prohibited it in machine-readable form), whereas the EU AI Act requires active compliance with copyright law and transparency about training data, representing a meaningfully different burden and standard.

Both require AI providers to comply with intellectual property law when obtaining training data, but the Beijing rule is a binding local regulation requiring legally obtained data without IP infringement, while the EU AI Act targets GPAI model providers and also requires transparency documentation.

rule_text: Developers of the most powerful AI models (systemic-risk GPAI) must conduct adversarial testing and red-teaming before releasing the model, and must report serious incidents to regulators.
rule_text_technical: Providers of general-purpose AI models posing systemic risk shall perform model evaluations in accordance with standardised protocols and adversarial testing of the model to identify and mitigate systemic risks; assess and mitigate possible systemic risks; keep track of, document and report serious incidents and possible corrective measures.

first_instance.law_name: EU AI Act, Art. 55

instances.notes: First binding pre-release adversarial testing and incident-reporting requirement for frontier AI models.
Frontier model developers must publish safety policies and conduct pre-deployment safety evaluations, but no formal redteaming requirement.
Requires algorithmic impact assessment prior to deployment but focused on discrimination/bias, not broader systemic safety risks.

instances.citation: Part V, Principle 2 – Safety and Security
instances.notes: Both address identifying and addressing security vulnerabilities and unwanted harms in AI systems, but the UNESCO rule is a broad voluntary lifecycle principle while the EU AI Act binding rule targets adversarial testing of high-risk GPAI models.

instances.citation: Measures Table — Validity and Robustness, Row 2
instances.notes: Both require adversarial testing and red-teaming of powerful AI systems, but the EU AI Act is binding and applies specifically to systemic-risk GPAI models, while this voluntary Canadian rule more broadly recommends adversarial testing for all advanced generative AI developers.

instances.citation: Part I, Principle 2 / Part II, Action 2
instances.notes: Both require post-deployment monitoring and vulnerability/incident response for advanced AI systems, but the EU AI Act is a binding mandate for systemic-risk GPAI while the G7 rule is a voluntary recommendation with broader scope including misuse patterns.

Both require assessment/testing of high-risk AI systems before operation, but Vietnam mandates a formal conformity assessment process, whereas the EU AI Act focuses on adversarial testing and red-teaming for systemic-risk GPAI models specifically.

Both address evaluating AI systems for safety risks and ensuring residual risks are within tolerance, but EU AI Act is binding and focused on systemic-risk GPAI while NIST RMF is voluntary and broader.

Both require testing AI systems under adversarial and edge-case conditions before deployment, but the EU AI Act is binding and applies to systemic-risk GPAI models specifically, while the ASEAN guide is a voluntary recommendation for organizations generally.

Both address oversight requirements for large-scale AI models trained on sensitive data, but this rule mandates a pre-training ethics review in China's S&T framework, while the EU AI Act requires adversarial testing and red-teaming for systemic-risk GPAI models.

instances.citation: Section V, AI Safety Research – Frontier AI
instances.notes: Both address frontier AI safety measures including identifying and mitigating catastrophic risks, but the EU AI Act is binding on systemic-risk GPAI providers while this is a voluntary call for leading AI developers.

rule_text: A 'high-risk AI system' is any AI that makes or materially influences consequential decisions affecting someone's education, employment, financial services, healthcare, housing, insurance, or legal rights.
rule_text_technical: A 'high-risk artificial intelligence system' means an artificial intelligence system that is specifically intended to autonomously make, or be a substantial factor in making, a consequential decision. A 'consequential decision' means a decision that has a material legal or similarly significant effect on the provision or denial to any consumer of education, employment, financial or lending services, essential government services, healthcare, housing, insurance, or legal services.

first_instance.law_name: Colorado SB 24-205 (Colorado AI Act), § 6-1-1702

instances.notes: First US state 'high-risk AI' definition anchored to consequential decision domains; influenced subsequent state bills.
EU uses a sector-and-use-case list (Annex III) rather than a consequential-decision definition; covers similar domains but is more prescriptive.
Texas TRAIGA copies the Colorado consequential-decision definition and sector list near-verbatim.
Washington AI Act lifts the Colorado definition and sector list almost word-for-word.
High-risk AI defined by potential for severe, widespread, or irreversible harm, plus sectoral lists; similar domains, different framing.

Both establish risk classification for AI systems, but Kazakhstan uses a three-tier (minimum/medium/high) scheme based on degree of risk, while Colorado's definition focuses on consequential decisions affecting specific life domains.

Both establish risk-based classification for AI systems, but Vietnam uses a three-tier (high/medium/low) system based on impact on human rights, safety, and security, whereas Colorado's definition focuses on consequential decisions affecting specific life domains.

Both address impact assessments and human oversight for medium/high-risk AI systems, but Colorado SB205 is a binding law defining high-risk AI in consequential decision contexts, while the ASEAN guide is a voluntary recommendation for Tier 2 medium-risk systems with lighter-touch requirements.

Both rules define high-stakes AI use cases affecting employment, education, and similar consequential decisions, but the Guangdong rule is broader in framing obligations rather than just defining scope.

Both classify AI used in medical diagnosis and treatment recommendations as high-risk, though Colorado's definition is broader (consequential decisions) and Utah's is scoped to direct consumer communications.

Both require classification of AI systems by risk category; Colorado defines 'high-risk AI' for consequential decisions while Peru mandates a four-tier classification (prohibited, high-risk, limited-risk, minimal-risk) by providers and deployers.

rule_text: Performers have the right to control and be compensated for any AI-generated reproduction of their voice, likeness, or digital replica. Using a performer's voice or likeness in AI-generated content without consent is a civil offence.
rule_text_technical: No person shall use an algorithm, artificial intelligence, digital replica or other technology to perform a recorded action of a performing artist without the express written consent of the performing artist or the artist's representative in connection with a commercial recording, audiovisual work or transmission.

first_instance.law_name: Tennessee ELVIS Act, § 47-25-1103

instances.notes: First US law specifically protecting performer voice and likeness against AI-generated reproduction; triggered by the proliferation of AI voice cloning tools.
Washington law grants individuals the right against AI-generated digital replicas of their voice or likeness without consent.
TAKE IT DOWN Act focuses specifically on intimate images; broader voice/likeness protection is out of scope.
AI-generated deepfakes must be disclosed; no performer-specific right of control, but transparency obligation applies.
