instances.notes: Rule introduced in Wisconsin 2023 Act 123 (AI Political Disclosures) (Wisconsin, 2024-03-21).

instances.citation: KRS Chapter 117 (new section) — conspicuous disclosure affirmative defense
instances.notes: Wisconsin's rule states that compliance does not shield from other liability, while Kentucky's rule creates an affirmative defense to civil liability when a conspicuous disclosure is made — these address related but meaningfully different liability consequences.

rule_text: You may be subject to a forfeiture of up to $1,000 per violation if you intentionally violate the audio or video disclosure requirements, enforced as provided under s. 11.1400(5).
rule_text_technical: Notwithstanding s. 11.1401(1)(b), whoever intentionally violates par. (b) or (c) shall be subject to a forfeiture not to exceed $1,000 for each violation. Any violation of par. (b) or (c) shall be enforced as provided under s. 11.1400(5).

first_instance.law_name: Wisconsin 2023 Act 123 — AI Disclosures in Political Communications

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Wisconsin 2023 Act 123 (AI Political Disclosures) (Wisconsin, 2024-03-21).

Both impose criminal/financial penalties for intentional violations of synthetic media political advertising rules, but Arizona imposes Class 1 misdemeanor criminal liability (elevated to felony for repeat offenses) while Wisconsin imposes civil forfeitures up to $1,000.

Both rules impose financial penalties for violations of AI disclosure requirements in political/election communications, but Singapore's rule also includes criminal offence liability whereas Wisconsin's rule is limited to civil forfeiture.

Both impose liability on the sponsor of a synthetic media election communication, but Wisconsin focuses on forfeitures for intentional violations while Kentucky creates civil liability specifically for sponsors who authorize the communication.

Both rules impose civil penalties for violations of AI disclosure requirements in political communications, but Michigan distinguishes between first violations (up to $1,000) and subsequent violations, while Wisconsin sets a flat $1,000 per violation forfeiture for intentional violations.

rule_text: Broadcasters and other hosts or carriers of audio or video communications containing synthetic media are not liable for disclosure violations under this subsection, unless they are the committee responsible for the communication.
rule_text_technical: No liability for a violation of this subsection shall attach to any person who is a broadcaster or other host or carrier of a video or audio communication described in sub. (2)(a) or (b) that contains synthetic media, unless the person is a committee responsible for the communication.

first_instance.law_name: Wisconsin 2023 Act 123 — AI Disclosures in Political Communications

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Wisconsin 2023 Act 123 (AI Political Disclosures) (Wisconsin, 2024-03-21).
Both rules exempt interactive computer service providers / broadcasters and carriers from liability when they merely publish or transmit third-party content containing synthetic or AI-altered media.
Both exempt broadcasters that were paid to air synthetic media content from liability when they make required disclosures, consistent with the pass-through broadcaster exemption pattern.

Both provide safe harbor protections for platforms regarding AI-generated political content, but NC's safe harbor is conditional on establishing and enforcing takedown policies, while WI's safe harbor is unconditional for broadcasters and carriers not responsible for creating the content.

instances.citation: KRS Chapter 117 (new section) — medium and advertising sales representative exemption
instances.notes: Both independently exempt media carriers and advertising intermediaries from liability for a sponsor's synthetic media election communication violations, drafted differently but reaching the same substantive result.

Both rules exempt broadcasters and carriers from liability for AI disclosure violations in third-party political content they carry, reflecting the same substantive standard of pass-through immunity for distribution infrastructure.

rule_text: This subsection must not be interpreted to alter or negate the rights, obligations, or immunities of interactive computer service providers under 47 U.S.C. 230.
rule_text_technical: This subsection may not be construed to alter or negate any rights, obligations, or immunities of a provider of an interactive computer service under 47 USC 230.

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Wisconsin 2023 Act 123 (AI Political Disclosures) (Wisconsin, 2024-03-21).
Both explicitly exempt interactive computer services as defined in 47 U.S.C. § 230 from synthetic media political advertising disclosure obligations.

rule_text: You cannot create, distribute, publish, or transmit an AI-generated replica of an individual for the purpose of defaming, harassing, extorting, or otherwise harming that individual without their prior written consent.
rule_text_technical: No person may, without the prior written consent of the individual or their authorized representative, create, distribute, publish, or transmit an AI-generated replica of an individual for the purpose of defaming, harassing, extorting, or otherwise harming that individual.

first_instance.law_name: Georgia Artificial Intelligence in Creative Content Act

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Georgia SB 396 (AI Likeness Protection) (Georgia, 2024-04-18).

Both prohibit creating/distributing deceptive AI-generated content involving real individuals, but the NC rule is specific to election advertisements and candidates while the GA rule focuses on defamation via AI-generated replicas.

rule_text: You cannot use an AI-generated replica of an individual to falsely imply that the individual endorses, authorizes, or approves any product, service, political candidate, or cause without their prior written consent.
rule_text_technical: No person may, without the prior written consent of the individual or their authorized representative, use an AI-generated replica of an individual to falsely imply that the individual endorses, authorizes, or approves any product, service, political candidate, or cause.

first_instance.law_name: Georgia Artificial Intelligence in Creative Content Act

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Georgia SB 396 (AI Likeness Protection) (Georgia, 2024-04-18).

Both rules address AI-generated impersonation of real individuals, but the Singapore rule is specifically targeted at candidates in election advertising contexts using voice/facial synthesis, while the Georgia rule broadly covers false endorsement via AI replicas.

Both prohibit using AI-generated replicas/synthetic content to falsely imply endorsement or impersonate individuals, but PA Act 35 specifically targets financial exploitation/fraud via synthetic voices, images, or videos, while GA SB396 focuses on false endorsement more broadly as a civil tort.

Both rules prohibit AI-based impersonation and deceptive use of deepfakes, but Colombia's rule is a binding criminal provision targeting fraud and financial crime via voice/face synthesis, while the Georgia rule is a civil tort remedy for false endorsement using AI replicas.

rule_text: The plaintiff must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the AI-generated replica depicts them, that the defendant created or distributed it without consent, and that the replica meets the statutory definition.
rule_text_technical: The plaintiff bears the burden of establishing by a preponderance of the evidence that the AI-generated replica depicts the plaintiff, that the defendant created or distributed it without consent, and that the replica meets the definition set forth in § 51-5-10.

first_instance.law_name: Georgia Artificial Intelligence in Creative Content Act

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Georgia SB 396 (AI Likeness Protection) (Georgia, 2024-04-18).

Both rules require a plaintiff to prove specific elements of an AI-generated/digital impersonation claim by a defined evidentiary standard, but Arizona's rule applies to election-related digital impersonation while Georgia's targets defamation and false endorsement contexts.

rule_text: You are exempt from liability under this chapter when using AI-generated replicas in historical or documentary works.
rule_text_technical: This chapter does not apply to uses of AI-generated replicas in historical or documentary works.

first_instance.law_name: Georgia Artificial Intelligence in Creative Content Act

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Georgia SB 396 (AI Likeness Protection) (Georgia, 2024-04-18).

Both exempt archival or documentary material from liability under AI-generated media laws, though Nevada's exemption applies in the election context and Georgia's applies to AI-generated replicas more broadly.

Both rules provide exemptions for historical/documentary use of AI-generated or digitally enhanced content, but Singapore's rule is scoped to digitally restored historical footage for documentary or educational purposes in the election advertising context, while Georgia's rule broadly covers historical or documentary works.

Both provide exemptions for news/documentary use of AI-generated replicas, but Arkansas also covers commentary and satire in the same exemption while Georgia's exemption is limited to historical or documentary works.

Both exempt news and documentary uses of AI-generated replicas from liability, but this rule applies specifically to deceased personalities and also covers advertising and commercial announcements for such works.

rule_text: You are exempt from liability under this chapter when using AI-generated replicas for educational or academic purposes.
rule_text_technical: This chapter does not apply to educational or academic uses of AI-generated replicas.

first_instance.law_name: Georgia Artificial Intelligence in Creative Content Act

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Georgia SB 396 (AI Likeness Protection) (Georgia, 2024-04-18).
Both exempt educational and academic use of AI-generated content from liability under their respective publicity/likeness rights frameworks, with substantively the same standard.

Both exempt commentary, criticism, and educational uses of AI-generated replicas from liability, but this rule applies specifically to digital replicas of deceased personalities and includes satire and parody.

rule_text: You must adopt or maintain appropriate legislative, administrative, or other measures to give effect to the Convention, graduated and differentiated according to the severity and probability of adverse impacts on human rights, democracy, and the rule of law.
rule_text_technical: Each Party shall adopt or maintain appropriate legislative, administrative or other measures to give effect to the provisions set out in this Convention, graduated and differentiated as may be necessary in view of the severity and probability of the occurrence of adverse impacts on human rights, democracy and the rule of law throughout the lifecycle of artificial intelligence systems, including specific or horizontal measures irrespective of the type of technology used.

first_instance.law_name: Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and Rule of Law

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Council of Europe AI Convention (Council of Europe, 2024-05-17).

Both require consistent protective measures across jurisdictions for AI systems, but the EU AI Act is a binding regulation imposing specific uniform standards across the EU internal market, while the CoE Convention requires parties to adopt appropriate measures and is broader in geographic/institutional scope.

rule_text: You must apply this Convention to activities within the lifecycle of AI systems undertaken by public authorities or private actors acting on their behalf.
rule_text_technical: Each Party shall apply this Convention to the activities within the lifecycle of artificial intelligence systems undertaken by public authorities, or private actors acting on their behalf.

first_instance.law_name: Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and Rule of Law

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Council of Europe AI Convention (Council of Europe, 2024-05-17).

Both define the scope of an AI law covering the AI lifecycle, but Vietnam's law explicitly lists research, development, provision, deployment, and use, and includes related organizations and state management, whereas the CoE Convention focuses on public/private actors and human rights impacts.

Both address territorial scope of AI regulation, but Peru's rule covers persons domiciled in Peru developing/marketing AI, while the CoE Convention addresses lifecycle activities by public authorities or private actors acting on their behalf.

rule_text: You must address risks and impacts arising from private actors' AI lifecycle activities not covered by public authority obligations, in a manner conforming with the Convention's object and purpose, and must declare how you intend to implement this obligation.
rule_text_technical: Each Party shall address risks and impacts arising from activities within the lifecycle of artificial intelligence systems by private actors to the extent not covered in subparagraph (a) in a manner conforming with the object and purpose of this Convention, specifying in a declaration submitted to the Secretary General of the Council of Europe at the time of signature or ratification how it intends to implement this obligation, either by applying Chapters II to VI principles and obligations to private actors or by taking other appropriate measures.

first_instance.law_name: Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and Rule of Law

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Council of Europe AI Convention (Council of Europe, 2024-05-17).

rule_text: When implementing obligations regarding private actors, you cannot derogate from or limit the application of your international obligations to protect human rights, democracy, and the rule of law.
rule_text_technical: When implementing the obligation under subparagraph (b), a Party may not derogate from or limit the application of its international obligations undertaken to protect human rights, democracy and the rule of law.

first_instance.law_name: Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and Rule of Law

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Council of Europe AI Convention (Council of Europe, 2024-05-17).

rule_text: You are not required to apply this Convention to AI lifecycle activities related to national security, provided those activities are conducted consistently with applicable international law including international human rights law and with respect for democratic institutions.
rule_text_technical: A Party shall not be required to apply this Convention to activities within the lifecycle of artificial intelligence systems related to the protection of its national security interests, with the understanding that such activities are conducted in a manner consistent with applicable international law, including international human rights law obligations, and with respect for its democratic institutions and processes.

first_instance.law_name: Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and Rule of Law

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Council of Europe AI Convention (Council of Europe, 2024-05-17).
Both exempt national defense/security AI activities from the law's scope, though Vietnam also adds 'cipher purposes' as a specific exemption category.

rule_text: You do not need to apply this Convention to AI research and development activities not yet made available for use, unless testing or similar activities could interfere with human rights, democracy, or the rule of law.
rule_text_technical: Without prejudice to Article 13 and Article 25(2), this Convention shall not apply to research and development activities regarding artificial intelligence systems not yet made available for use, unless testing or similar activities are undertaken in such a way that they have the potential to interfere with human rights, democracy and the rule of law.

first_instance.law_name: Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and Rule of Law

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Council of Europe AI Convention (Council of Europe, 2024-05-17).

rule_text: Matters relating to national defence do not fall within the scope of this Convention and are entirely excluded.
rule_text_technical: Matters relating to national defence do not fall within the scope of this Convention.

first_instance.law_name: Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and Rule of Law

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Council of Europe AI Convention (Council of Europe, 2024-05-17).

rule_text: You must adopt or maintain measures to protect democratic processes in the context of AI lifecycle activities, including individuals' fair access to and participation in public debate and their ability to freely form opinions.
rule_text_technical: Each Party shall adopt or maintain measures that seek to protect its democratic processes in the context of activities within the lifecycle of artificial intelligence systems, including individuals' fair access to and participation in public debate, as well as their ability to freely form opinions.

first_instance.law_name: Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and Rule of Law

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Council of Europe AI Convention (Council of Europe, 2024-05-17).
Both address designing AI to respect rule of law, human rights, and democratic values, but the CoE Convention is binding and more specific about democratic process protections.

Both concern protecting democratic content/processes, but the OSA is a binding platform-level content protection duty while the CoE convention is a state-level obligation to protect democratic processes from AI lifecycle activities.

rule_text: Individuals have the right to bring a civil action for digital impersonation within two years after they know, or reasonably should know, that a digital impersonation of them was published.
rule_text_technical: A candidate for public office or political party office who will appear on the ballot in Arizona, or any citizen of Arizona, may bring an action for digital impersonation within two years after the date that the person knows, or in the exercise of reasonable diligence should know, that a digital impersonation of the person who is bringing the action was published.

Both provide civil action rights to individuals depicted in deceptive digital/synthetic media, but SB1359 specifically covers candidates depicted in political advertising deepfakes while HB2394 covers broader digital impersonation.

Both grant candidates/individuals the right to bring a civil action for AI-generated deceptive depictions, but Nevada limits standing to candidates depicted in election-related media while Arizona's digital impersonation right is broader and includes a two-year limitations period.

rule_text: If the digital impersonation is part of a paid advertisement, you can only bring a cause of action against the person or entity that originated, ordered, placed, or paid for the advertisement.
rule_text_technical: If the digital impersonation is or is part of a paid advertisement, a cause of action for digital impersonation may be brought only against the person or entity that originated, ordered, placed or paid for the advertisement.

first_instance.law_name: Arizona HB 2394 — Digitally Altered Media; Civil Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Arizona HB 2394 (Deepfake Civil Remedies) (Arizona, 2024-05-21).

rule_text: A plaintiff bringing a digital impersonation action must make diligent efforts to both serve and provide prompt actual notice to all defendants.
rule_text_technical: A person who brings an action for digital impersonation may file a complaint and a motion for preliminary declaratory relief in the superior court; the plaintiff shall make diligent efforts to both serve and provide prompt actual notice to all defendants.

first_instance.law_name: Arizona HB 2394 — Digitally Altered Media; Civil Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Arizona HB 2394 (Deepfake Civil Remedies) (Arizona, 2024-05-21).

rule_text: Preliminary declaratory relief may only be granted against a non-appearing defendant if the plaintiff's complaint is verified and a declaration is filed explaining why, with reasonable diligence, the defendant could not be served.
rule_text_technical: Preliminary declaratory relief may be granted against a defendant who does not appear only if the plaintiff's complaint is verified and a declaration is filed that states why with the exercise of reasonable diligence the defendant could not be served.

first_instance.law_name: Arizona HB 2394 — Digitally Altered Media; Civil Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Arizona HB 2394 (Deepfake Civil Remedies) (Arizona, 2024-05-21).

rule_text: Preliminary declaratory relief may only be granted if the plaintiff proves the elements of digital impersonation and at least one of the following: the plaintiff is a candidate with an election within 180 days; the impersonation depicts sexual content; it depicts a criminal act; the plaintiff would suffer significant personal or financial hardship without relief; or the plaintiff's reputation will be irreparably harmed.
rule_text_technical: Preliminary declaratory relief may be granted only if the plaintiff proves the elements of digital impersonation prescribed by subsection A and at least one of the following: (1) the person is a candidate with an election scheduled within 180 days; (2) the digital impersonation depicts the person engaging in a sexual act or depicts unclothed breasts, buttocks or genitals; (3) the digital impersonation depicts the person engaging in a criminal act; (4) in the absence of preliminary relief, the person can reasonably be expected to suffer significant personal or financial hardship or loss of employment opportunities; or (5) in the absence of preliminary relief, the person's reputation will be irreparably harmed.

first_instance.law_name: Arizona HB 2394 — Digitally Altered Media; Civil Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Arizona HB 2394 (Deepfake Civil Remedies) (Arizona, 2024-05-21).

rule_text: If the defendant does not appear, contest the claim, and no other party intervenes as a defendant, the plaintiff is not entitled to taxable costs.
rule_text_technical: If the defendant does not appear and contest the claim and no other party intervenes as a defendant, the plaintiff is not entitled to taxable costs.

first_instance.law_name: Arizona HB 2394 — Digitally Altered Media; Civil Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Arizona HB 2394 (Deepfake Civil Remedies) (Arizona, 2024-05-21).

rule_text: If a defendant has not been served within 90 days after filing and no party has appeared or intervened as a defendant, the claims against that defendant must be dismissed and any preliminary relief granted expires, unless the court finds the interests of justice require otherwise.
rule_text_technical: If a defendant has not been served within ninety days after the date of filing and no party has appeared or intervened as a defendant in intervention, the claims against that defendant shall be dismissed and any preliminary relief that was granted shall expire unless the court finds that the interests of justice require otherwise.

first_instance.law_name: Arizona HB 2394 — Digitally Altered Media; Civil Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Arizona HB 2394 (Deepfake Civil Remedies) (Arizona, 2024-05-21).

rule_text: In addition to declaratory relief, a plaintiff may obtain injunctive relief and damages only if the digital impersonation depicts sexual content appealing to prurient interests and offending community standards, the plaintiff was not a public figure, and the publication was made with actual knowledge it was a digital impersonation or the publisher failed to take reasonable corrective action within 21 days of gaining actual knowledge.
rule_text_technical: In addition to declaratory relief, a plaintiff in an action for digital impersonation may obtain injunctive relief and damages only if the elements of digital impersonation in subsection A and all of the following are proven: (1) the digital impersonation depicts the person engaging in a sexual act or depicts unclothed breasts, buttocks or genitals, appeals to prurient interests and offends local community standards; (2) the plaintiff was not a public figure, including a limited public figure, at the time the cause of action accrued; and (3) the publication was made with actual knowledge that the recording or image was a digital impersonation or the publisher failed to take reasonable corrective action within twenty-one days after having actual knowledge.

first_instance.law_name: Arizona HB 2394 — Digitally Altered Media; Civil Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Arizona HB 2394 (Deepfake Civil Remedies) (Arizona, 2024-05-21).

Both provide for injunctive relief and actual damages for AI-generated deceptive media, but Nevada explicitly includes lost campaign contributions and reputational harm as recoverable damages while Arizona's damages are more general.

rule_text: If a publisher gains actual knowledge that content is a digital impersonation, they must take reasonable corrective action within 21 days, which includes removing or disabling access to the digital impersonation and publishing a statement to the same audience that the publication was a digital impersonation.
rule_text_technical: Reasonable corrective action includes removing or disabling access to the digital impersonation and publishing to the same audience a statement that the publication was a digital impersonation; failure to take such corrective action within twenty-one days after actual knowledge subjects the publisher to liability for injunctive relief and damages.

first_instance.law_name: Arizona HB 2394 — Digitally Altered Media; Civil Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Arizona HB 2394 (Deepfake Civil Remedies) (Arizona, 2024-05-21).

rule_text: Factual or legal determinations made by the court in granting preliminary declaratory relief may not be considered by the trier of fact or the court at any later stage of the proceeding or in any other proceeding.
rule_text_technical: If preliminary declaratory relief is granted, any factual or legal determinations made by the court shall not be considered by the trier of fact or the court at any later stage of the proceeding or in any other proceeding.

first_instance.law_name: Arizona HB 2394 — Digitally Altered Media; Civil Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Arizona HB 2394 (Deepfake Civil Remedies) (Arizona, 2024-05-21).

rule_text: The standard of proof for preliminary declaratory relief and injunctive relief and damages is clear and convincing evidence; for permanent declaratory relief, the standard is a preponderance of the evidence.
rule_text_technical: The standard of proof for actions under this section is: (1) for preliminary declaratory relief, clear and convincing evidence; (2) for injunctive relief and damages, clear and convincing evidence; (3) for permanent declaratory relief, a preponderance of the evidence.

first_instance.law_name: Arizona HB 2394 — Digitally Altered Media; Civil Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Arizona HB 2394 (Deepfake Civil Remedies) (Arizona, 2024-05-21).

rule_text: A plaintiff must file a complaint in the superior court for the county in which the plaintiff resides, or if the plaintiff is a presidential candidate, in Maricopa County or any county where one of the candidate's political party's electors resides.
rule_text_technical: A plaintiff who brings an action under this section may file a complaint in the superior court for the county in which the plaintiff resides or, if the plaintiff is a candidate for President of the United States, in Maricopa County or in any county in which one of the candidate's political party's appointees for elector resides.

first_instance.law_name: Arizona HB 2394 — Digitally Altered Media; Civil Action

rule_text: A parent or guardian of a minor child or incapacitated person may seek relief under this section on behalf of the minor child or incapacitated person.
rule_text_technical: A parent or guardian of a minor child or incapacitated person may seek relief under this section on the minor child's or incapacitated person's behalf.

rule_text: Interactive computer services, electronic mail service providers, telecommunications service providers, information service providers, and access software providers are exempt from liability under this Section for acts committed by users on their platforms.
rule_text_technical: The provisions of this Section shall not apply to an interactive computer service, electronic mail service provider, or a provider of a telecommunications service or any information service as defined in 47 U.S.C. 153, system, or access software provider that provides or enables computer access by multiple users to a computer server that was used by a person to commit any act prohibited by Subsection A of this Section.

rule_text: You must comply with a uniform legal framework governing the development, placing on the market, putting into service, and use of AI systems in the Union.
rule_text_technical: This Regulation lays down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence applicable to the development, placing on the market, putting into service, and use of AI systems in the Union, ensuring free movement of AI-based goods and services and preventing Member States from imposing restrictions unless explicitly authorised.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

Both rules impose compliance obligations under the EU AI Act framework, but this rule specifically concerns obedience to Danish market surveillance remedial orders with time limits, which is a national enforcement implementation detail beyond the general EU AI Act compliance obligation.

Both establish the scope of AI Act compliance obligations, but the Hungarian rule specifies the domestic implementation context and enumerates the specific actor categories (provider, deployer, importer, distributor, authorized representative) subject to the Act.

Both provide transitional obligations for AI systems already in operation when the law takes effect, but Vietnam's rule specifically grants a compliance period for existing systems, while the EU AI Act establishes a phased application timeline for new obligations.

Both require AI systems to comply with technical requirements and quality standards, but Peru's rule is a developer/marketer obligation while the EU AI Act establishes a comprehensive uniform legal framework.

Peru's high-risk classification for safety components of critical infrastructure mirrors the EU AI Act's high-risk category, but is adopted independently in binding Peruvian law rather than as part of the EU framework.

rule_text: Your obligations under this Regulation apply without prejudice to existing Union law on data protection, consumer protection, fundamental rights, employment, product safety, and the right to compensation under applicable liability rules.
rule_text_technical: The harmonised rules apply across sectors and are without prejudice to existing Union law, including on data protection, consumer protection, fundamental rights, employment and protection of workers, and product safety; all rights and remedies under such Union law, including compensation pursuant to Council Directive 85/374/EEC, remain unaffected and fully applicable.

rule_text: You must clearly disclose in writing to each tenant, prior to lease signing, whether the rental property is located in a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area ('100-year floodplain') and, if you have actual knowledge, whether the property or its parking areas have experienced flooding and the frequency of such flooding.
rule_text_technical: Every landlord shall clearly disclose to each tenant in writing prior to signing the lease that a rental property is located in the FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area ('100-year floodplain') and, if the landlord has actual knowledge, that the rental property or any portion of the parking areas has been subjected to flooding and the frequency thereof.

rule_text: If you lease a lower-level unit, you must clearly disclose in writing to the tenant prior to lease signing whether the lower-level unit or any portion of the property has experienced flooding in the last 10 years and the frequency of such flooding.
rule_text_technical: Every landlord who leases a lower-level unit shall clearly disclose to each lower-level unit tenant in writing prior to the signing of the lease whether the lower-level unit or any portion of the real property containing the lower-level unit has experienced flooding in the last 10 years and shall disclose the frequency of such flooding.

first_instance.law_name: Illinois Artificial Intelligence Video Interview Act — Extended to Employment Analytics

first_instance.law_name: Illinois Artificial Intelligence Video Interview Act — Extended to Employment Analytics

rule_text: If you fail to disclose FEMA flood zone status and the tenant subsequently discovers this, the tenant has the right to terminate the lease by written notice within 30 days of discovering the non-disclosure, and you must return all prepaid rent and fees within 15 days of receiving that notice.
rule_text_technical: If a landlord fails to comply with subsection (b) and the tenant subsequently becomes aware that the property is located in the FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area, the tenant may terminate the lease by giving written notice no later than the 30th day after becoming aware of the non-compliance, and the landlord shall return all rent and fees paid in advance no later than the 15th day after the tenant gave notice.

rule_text: You must include a reasonably specific description of the intended uses of the digital replica in any contract provision authorizing such use, or the provision risks being unenforceable.
rule_text_technical: Except as provided in § 927(a)(2)(B), a provision is unenforceable if it does not include a reasonably specific description of the intended uses of the digital replica.

first_instance.law_name: Contracts Involving AI Replicas of Performers Act

Both require consent before using AI to produce a digital likeness of an individual, but PA Act 35 is a criminal statute requiring consent for any AI-generated digital likeness, while CA AB2602 is a contract-law instrument requiring specific description of intended uses in agreements involving digital replicas.

rule_text: You are not required to include a reasonably specific description of intended uses of a digital replica if those uses are consistent with the terms of the contract for personal or professional services and the fundamental character of the photography or soundtrack as recorded or performed.
rule_text_technical: Failure to include a reasonably specific description of the intended uses of a digital replica does not render the provision unenforceable if the uses are consistent with the terms of the contract for the performance of personal or professional services and the fundamental character of the photography or soundtrack as recorded or performed.

first_instance.law_name: Contracts Involving AI Replicas of Performers Act

instances.notes: Rule introduced in California AB 2602 (AI in Entertainment Contracts) (California, 2024-09-17).

rule_text: A digital replica contract provision remains enforceable if the individual was represented by legal counsel who negotiated on their behalf and the commercial terms are stated clearly and conspicuously in a signed or initialed contract or writing.
rule_text_technical: A provision is not rendered unenforceable under § 927(a)(3) if the individual was represented by legal counsel who negotiated on behalf of the individual licensing the individual's digital replica rights, and the commercial terms are stated clearly and conspicuously in a contract or other writing signed or initialed by the individual.

first_instance.law_name: Contracts Involving AI Replicas of Performers Act

instances.notes: Rule introduced in California AB 2602 (AI in Entertainment Contracts) (California, 2024-09-17).

rule_text: Unenforceability under this statute applies only to the specific digital replica provision at issue and does not affect other provisions of the contract, including any exclusivity grants related to that provision.
rule_text_technical: This section does not affect provisions of a contract other than a provision that falls under subdivision (a) and does not impact, abrogate, or otherwise affect any exclusivity grants contained in, or related to, a provision subject to subdivision (a).

first_instance.law_name: Contracts Involving AI Replicas of Performers Act

instances.notes: Rule introduced in California AB 2602 (AI in Entertainment Contracts) (California, 2024-09-17).

rule_text: Electronic reproduction, sampling, remixing, mastering, or digital remastering of a sound recording or audiovisual work authorized by the copyright holder is not considered a 'digital replica' under this statute.
rule_text_technical: 'Digital replica' does not include the electronic reproduction, use of a sample of one sound recording or audiovisual work into another, remixing, mastering, or digital remastering of a sound recording or audiovisual work authorized by the copyright holder.

first_instance.law_name: Contracts Involving AI Replicas of Performers Act

rule_text: You must make available, at no cost to users, an AI detection tool that allows users to assess whether image, video, or audio content was created or altered by your GenAI system, outputs system provenance data, and supports both URL and upload-based access as well as an API.
rule_text_technical: A covered provider shall make available an AI detection tool at no cost to the user that: (1) allows a user to assess whether image, video, or audio content, or content that is any combination thereof, was created or altered by the covered provider's GenAI system; (2) outputs any system provenance data detected in the content; (3) does not output any personal provenance data detected in the content; (4) is publicly accessible, subject to reasonable limitations to prevent demonstrable security or integrity risks; (5) allows a user to upload content or provide a URL linking to online content; and (6) supports an API allowing invocation without visiting the covered provider's internet website.

first_instance.law_name: California AI Transparency Act

instances.notes: Rule introduced in California SB 942 (AI Transparency Act) (California, 2024-09-19).
Near-verbatim adoption of California SB 942's requirement to provide a free AI detection tool for image, video, or audio content.

instances.citation: Technical Standards and Interoperability — API Exposure for Fact-Checkers
instances.notes: Both require mechanisms to allow querying or detection of AI-generated content status, but this rule mandates API exposure specifically to authorized fact-checking organizations, while the California rule requires a free AI detection tool for general users.

rule_text: Your AI detection tool must output any system provenance data detected in submitted content.
rule_text_technical: The AI detection tool shall output any system provenance data that is detected in the content submitted by the user.

rule_text: Your AI detection tool must not output any personal provenance data detected in submitted content.

rule_text: You may impose reasonable limitations on access to your AI detection tool only to prevent or respond to demonstrable risks to the security or integrity of your GenAI system.
rule_text_technical: A covered provider may impose reasonable limitations on access to the AI detection tool to prevent, or respond to, demonstrable risks to the security or integrity of its GenAI system, notwithstanding the general requirement that the tool be publicly accessible.

first_instance.law_name: California AI Transparency Act

rule_text: You must collect user feedback on the efficacy of your AI detection tool and incorporate relevant feedback into efforts to improve the tool.

first_instance.law_name: California AI Transparency Act

rule_text: You must not retain any personal provenance data from content submitted to your AI detection tool by a user.
rule_text_technical: A covered provider shall not retain any personal provenance data from content submitted to the AI detection tool by a user.

first_instance.law_name: California AI Transparency Act

rule_text: The latent disclosure you include in AI-generated content must be detectable by your own AI detection tool.

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Malaysia PDPA Amendment 2024 (Malaysia, 2024-10-09).

instances.citation: Data Breach Notification — Controller to Data Subjects
instances.notes: Serbia's requirement to notify data subjects of high-risk breaches without undue delay mirrors GDPR Art. 34 and Malaysia's PDPA s.12B(2) obligation to notify affected individuals.
Both require direct notification to affected data subjects when a personal data breach is likely to cause significant harm to them.

instances.citation: PDPL Art. (Data Breach Notification) – Notification to Data Subjects
instances.notes: Both require notification to affected data subjects when a personal data breach poses a high risk of significant harm.
Both require notifying affected individuals when a breach is likely to cause significant or high risk of harm to them.
Both require direct notification to affected data subjects when a breach presents a high risk of significant harm to their rights and freedoms.

instances.citation: UU PDP Art. (Data Breach Notification — Data Subjects)
instances.notes: Both require notification to affected data subjects when a personal data breach is likely to cause significant harm, with notification required as soon as practicable after discovery.

instances.citation: NDPA 2023, Data Breach Notification — Data Subjects
instances.notes: Both require notification to affected data subjects when a breach is likely to result in significant harm or high risk to those individuals.
Both require notification to affected data subjects without undue delay when a breach is likely to cause significant harm, mirroring GDPR Art. 34 requirements.
Both require notification to affected data subjects without undue delay when a personal data breach is likely to result in high risk to their rights.
Both require communicating high-risk personal data breaches to affected data subjects without undue delay.
Both require notification to affected data subjects in cases of high-risk or significant-harm breaches.
Both require notification to affected data subjects of a security breach in a prescribed manner with specific required information.
Both require notifying affected individuals of a privacy breach that is likely to cause significant/serious harm, as soon as practicable.

rule_text: If you fail to notify the Commissioner of a personal data breach as required, you commit an offence and may be liable on conviction to a fine not exceeding two hundred and fifty thousand ringgit, imprisonment for up to two years, or both.
rule_text_technical: A data controller who contravenes subsection (1) commits an offence and shall, on conviction, be liable to a fine not exceeding two hundred and fifty thousand ringgit or imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years or to both.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Act 2024 (Act A1727)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Malaysia PDPA Amendment 2024 (Malaysia, 2024-10-09).

Both make failure to notify the supervisory authority of a privacy breach an offence, but NZ § 118 specifies a fine as the maximum penalty while Malaysia's provision uses 'liable on conviction' language.

rule_text: Individuals have the right to request that their personal data be transmitted directly to another data controller of their choice by giving written notice via electronic means.
rule_text_technical: Subject to subsection (2), a data subject may request the data controller to transmit his personal data to another data controller of his choice directly by giving a notice in writing by way of electronic means to the data controller.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Act 2024 (Act A1727)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Malaysia PDPA Amendment 2024 (Malaysia, 2024-10-09).
Serbia's data portability right mirrors GDPR Art. 20 and Malaysia's PDPA s.43A — individuals may receive their data in a structured, machine-readable format.

Both establish the right to data portability — receiving personal data in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format — though Egypt's rule does not explicitly mention direct transmission to another controller.

instances.citation: PDPL Art. (Data Subject Rights) – Right to Portability
instances.notes: Both establish a right to data portability, allowing individuals to receive their personal data in a machine-readable format for transfer to another controller.
Both grant a right to receive personal data in a structured, machine-readable format and to have it transmitted to another controller; the UAE rule uses nearly identical GDPR-style language.
Both establish the right to receive personal data in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format and to transmit it to another controller.

instances.citation: UU PDP Art. (Right to Data Portability)
instances.notes: Both grant individuals the right to receive their personal data in a structured, machine-readable format and to have it transmitted to another controller.
Both provide individuals the right to receive personal data in a structured, machine-readable format and to transmit it to another controller.

instances.citation: § Rights of Data Subjects — Right to Data Portability
instances.notes: Both grant individuals the right to data portability — to receive personal data in a structured, machine-readable format and have it transmitted to another controller — consistent with GDPR Art. 20.

instances.citation: Ch. 501, Part V, F.S. — Consumer Rights (Right to Data Portability)
instances.notes: Both establish a right to receive personal data in a portable, usable format; Florida's version is a binding state statute while Malaysia's is a 2024 amendment with similar scope.
Both grant individuals the right to receive personal data in a structured, machine-readable format and to transmit it to another controller.

Both establish a right to data portability allowing individuals to receive their personal data in a structured format and transmit it to another controller where processing is based on consent or contract and carried out by automated means.

instances.citation: LFPDPPP 2025, Expanded Data Subject Rights — Right to Data Portability
instances.notes: Both establish a right to data portability including direct transfer to another controller in a structured, machine-readable format; Mexico's rule independently adopts the same substantive standard as Malaysia's PDPA amendment.
Both grant the right to receive personal data in a structured, machine-readable format and to transmit it to another controller.
Both establish a right to data portability enabling data subjects to receive their personal data in a portable format upon request, drafted differently but substantively equivalent.

Both rules concern data portability to third parties on user request, but the Data Act is broader (IoT/connected products, not personal data only) and adds structured format and free-of-charge requirements.

rule_text: The right to data portability is subject to technical feasibility and compatibility of data format.
rule_text_technical: The request for data portability referred to in subsection (1) is subject to technical feasibility and compatibility of the data format.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Act 2024 (Act A1727)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Malaysia PDPA Amendment 2024 (Malaysia, 2024-10-09).

rule_text: Upon receiving a data portability request, you must complete the transmission of personal data within the prescribed period.
rule_text_technical: Upon receiving the request for data portability under subsection (1), the data controller shall complete the transmission of personal data within the period as may be prescribed.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Act 2024 (Act A1727)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Malaysia PDPA Amendment 2024 (Malaysia, 2024-10-09).

rule_text: The Commissioner may issue subsidiary instruments, including by way of electronic means, in addition to other authorised methods.
rule_text_technical: Subsection 136(1) of the principal Act is amended by inserting after paragraph (a) the following paragraph: '(aa) by way of electronic means;', expanding the means by which the Commissioner may act.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Act 2024 (Act A1727)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Malaysia PDPA Amendment 2024 (Malaysia, 2024-10-09).

rule_text: You must ensure that products with digital elements placed on the Union market meet essential cybersecurity requirements, addressing vulnerabilities and providing security updates throughout the product lifecycle.
rule_text_technical: Manufacturers are required to ensure that hardware and software products with digital elements are placed on the market with fewer vulnerabilities and that security is maintained throughout a product's lifecycle, in accordance with the essential cybersecurity requirements established by this Regulation.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 on Cybersecurity Requirements for Products with Digital Elements

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Cyber Resilience Act (2024) (European Union, 2024-10-10).

Both rules extend liability/compliance frameworks to software including AI, but the CRA focuses on cybersecurity requirements while this rule establishes no-fault product liability for software/AI systems.

Both require cybersecurity measures including encryption and access controls, but this rule is sector-specific to robo-advisory financial services in Mauritius and is a voluntary instrument rather than EU binding regulation.

rule_text: You must provide users with clear information about the support period for your products with digital elements so they can make informed cybersecurity decisions.
rule_text_technical: Manufacturers shall create conditions enabling users to take cybersecurity into account when selecting and using products with digital elements, including by improving transparency with regard to the support period for products with digital elements made available on the market.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 on Cybersecurity Requirements for Products with Digital Elements

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Cyber Resilience Act (2024) (European Union, 2024-10-10).

rule_text: You must ensure the cybersecurity of products with digital elements that are only indirectly connected to other devices or networks, as cyber threats can propagate through chains of products.
rule_text_technical: Manufacturers shall ensure the cybersecurity of products with digital elements that are only indirectly connected to other devices or networks, given that cyber threats can propagate through various products with digital elements before reaching a certain target by chaining together multiple vulnerability exploits.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 on Cybersecurity Requirements for Products with Digital Elements

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Cyber Resilience Act (2024) (European Union, 2024-10-10).

rule_text: You must subject consumer products with digital elements categorised as 'important products' — such as smart door locks, baby monitoring systems, alarm systems, connected toys, and personal wearable health technology — to stricter conformity assessment procedures.
rule_text_technical: Consumer products with digital elements categorised as important products with digital elements, including smart home products with security functionalities such as smart door locks, baby monitoring systems, alarm systems, connected toys, and personal wearable health technology, shall undergo a stricter conformity assessment procedure due to the higher cybersecurity risk they present.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 on Cybersecurity Requirements for Products with Digital Elements

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Cyber Resilience Act (2024) (European Union, 2024-10-10).

rule_text: You must ensure that remote data processing solutions designed and developed by or on behalf of you — where the absence of such processing would prevent the product from performing one of its functions — comply with the cybersecurity requirements of this Regulation.
rule_text_technical: Manufacturers shall ensure that remote data processing solutions, defined as data processing at a distance for which the software is designed and developed by or on behalf of the manufacturer and the absence of which would prevent the product with digital elements from performing one of its functions, meet the applicable cybersecurity requirements under this Regulation, irrespective of whether data is processed or stored locally or remotely.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 on Cybersecurity Requirements for Products with Digital Elements

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Cyber Resilience Act (2024) (European Union, 2024-10-10).

rule_text: You cannot publish, cause to be published, or knowingly permit the publication of online election advertising that contains digitally generated or digitally manipulated depictions of a candidate's appearance, voice, words, or actions without a clear and prominent disclosure that the content has been digitally generated or manipulated.
rule_text_technical: No person may publish, cause to be published, or knowingly permit to be published any online election advertising that (1) contains digitally generated or digitally manipulated depictions of a candidate's appearance, voice, words, or actions; and (2) does not include a clear and prominent disclosure that the content has been digitally generated or manipulated. This prohibition applies regardless of whether content is published by the candidate, supporters, or any third party; whether the publishing platform is registered for OEA purposes; and whether the content was created with or without the depicted candidate's consent.

first_instance.law_name: Elections (Integrity of Online Advertising) (Amendment) Act 2024 (Singapore)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Singapore Elections (AI Integrity) Act 2024 (Singapore, 2024-10-15).

rule_text: You must include the required AI disclosure label on any AI-generated or AI-manipulated content depicting a candidate that is published or re-published during the election period, even if the content was originally created before that period.
rule_text_technical: The disclosure obligation for AI-generated content applies to content published during the election period (Nomination Day to Polling Day, inclusive), regardless of when the content was originally created. Content created before the election period that depicts a candidate and is re-published or shared during the election period must include the required AI disclosure label.

first_instance.law_name: Elections (Integrity of Online Advertising) (Amendment) Act 2024 (Singapore)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Singapore Elections (AI Integrity) Act 2024 (Singapore, 2024-10-15).

rule_text: You must comply with this Act's requirements if you publish covered content from within Singapore, or if you publish from outside Singapore but target Singapore voters, and you are a Singapore citizen, permanent resident, or Singapore-registered entity.
rule_text_technical: The Act applies to content published online that is (1) published from within Singapore; or (2) published from outside Singapore but targeted at Singapore voters or accessible to Singapore residents, where the publisher is a Singapore citizen, permanent resident, or Singapore-registered entity.

first_instance.law_name: Elections (Integrity of Online Advertising) (Amendment) Act 2024 (Singapore)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Singapore Elections (AI Integrity) Act 2024 (Singapore, 2024-10-15).

rule_text: The Returning Officer has the authority to issue take-down notices and correction direction orders to publishers of non-compliant AI-generated election advertising, refer cases to police, and seek urgent injunctive relief from courts.
rule_text_technical: The Returning Officer may: (1) issue take-down notices to publishers of non-compliant AI-generated election advertising; (2) issue correction direction orders requiring publishers to add the required disclosure label; (3) refer cases to the police for investigation and prosecution; and (4) apply to court for urgent injunctive relief to prevent continued publication.

first_instance.law_name: Elections (Integrity of Online Advertising) (Amendment) Act 2024 (Singapore)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Singapore Elections (AI Integrity) Act 2024 (Singapore, 2024-10-15).

rule_text: Online platforms that fail to comply with take-down or correction direction orders within the specified timeframe may themselves be held liable for the offence of publishing non-compliant election advertising, regardless of whether the platform created the content.
rule_text_technical: Online platforms that fail to comply with take-down or correction direction orders within the specified timeframe may be liable for the offence of publishing non-compliant election advertising, regardless of whether the platform created the content.

first_instance.law_name: Elections (Integrity of Online Advertising) (Amendment) Act 2024 (Singapore)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Singapore Elections (AI Integrity) Act 2024 (Singapore, 2024-10-15).

rule_text: AI-generated content published by or with the written consent of the depicted candidate is permitted, but must still comply with the mandatory disclosure requirements.
rule_text_technical: AI-generated content published by or with the prior written consent of the depicted candidate is exempt from the prohibition, subject to continued compliance with the disclosure requirements under Section 4.

first_instance.law_name: Elections (Integrity of Online Advertising) (Amendment) Act 2024 (Singapore)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Singapore Elections (AI Integrity) Act 2024 (Singapore, 2024-10-15).

rule_text: You cannot apply this Directive's product liability regime to damage arising from nuclear accidents where such damage is already covered by international conventions ratified by Member States.
rule_text_technical: Liability for defective products shall not apply to damage arising from nuclear accidents in so far as liability for such damage is covered by international conventions ratified by Member States.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

rule_text: Member States must not maintain or introduce national rules that are more stringent or less stringent than those laid down in this Directive in respect of matters within its scope.
rule_text_technical: In order to create a genuine internal market with a high and uniform level of protection of consumers and other natural persons, and to reflect the case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union, Member States shall not, in respect of matters within the scope of this Directive, maintain or introduce provisions that are more stringent or less stringent than those laid down in this Directive.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

rule_text: You must not treat information (e.g., content of digital files such as media files, e-books, or mere source code) as a 'product' for the purposes of product liability; only software constitutes a product.
rule_text_technical: Information is not to be considered a product, and product liability rules shall therefore not apply to the content of digital files, such as media files or e-books or the mere source code of software; software itself, including AI systems, is a product for the purposes of applying no-fault liability.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

rule_text: You cannot apply this Directive to free and open-source software developed or supplied outside the course of a commercial activity, as such software is not considered placed on the market.
rule_text_technical: This Directive shall not apply to free and open-source software developed or supplied outside the course of a commercial activity; however, where software is supplied in exchange for a price, or for personal data used other than exclusively for improving the security, compatibility or interoperability of the software, and is therefore supplied in the course of a commercial activity, this Directive shall apply.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

rule_text: You may be held liable as a manufacturer if you integrate free and open-source software into your product in the course of a commercial activity, even if the original open-source software developer is not liable.
rule_text_technical: Where free and open-source software supplied outside the course of a commercial activity is subsequently integrated by a manufacturer as a component into a product in the course of a commercial activity and is thereby placed on the market, it shall be possible to hold that manufacturer liable for damage caused by the defectiveness of such software; the manufacturer of the open-source software shall not be liable as it would not have fulfilled the conditions of placing a product or component on the market.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

rule_text: You must treat digital manufacturing files (e.g., CAD files for 3D printing) as 'products' subject to this Directive's liability regime when developed or supplied in the course of a commercial activity.
rule_text_technical: Digital manufacturing files, which contain the functional information necessary to produce a tangible item by enabling the automated control of machinery or tools, shall be considered products for the purposes of this Directive in order to ensure the protection of natural persons in cases where such files are defective, provided they are developed or supplied in the course of a commercial activity; raw materials such as gas, water, and electricity are also products.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

rule_text: You must treat integrated or inter-connected digital services that determine the safety of a product as components of that product, making them subject to no-fault liability rules where they are within the manufacturer's control.
rule_text_technical: No-fault liability shall be extended to digital services integrated into, or inter-connected with, a product in such a way that the absence of the service would prevent the product from performing one of its functions; those related services shall be considered components of the product into which they are integrated or with which they are inter-connected where they are within the control of the manufacturer of that product.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

rule_text: Liability without fault on the part of economic operators is the mandatory standard for addressing the apportionment of risk in modern technological production under this Directive.
rule_text_technical: Liability without fault on the part of economic operators remains the sole means of adequately addressing the problem of fair apportionment of risk inherent in modern technological production, forming the foundational principle of the liability regime established by this Directive.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

rule_text: This Directive does not affect national law provisions on contractual liability, fault-based liability, or other non-contractual liability that do not involve the manufacturer's liability for product defectiveness as established here.
rule_text_technical: National law provisions enabling an injured person to claim damages on the basis of contractual liability or on grounds of non-contractual liability that does not involve the manufacturer's liability for the defectiveness of a product as established in this Directive — such as liability based on a warranty, fault, or strict liability of operators for damage caused by properties of organisms resulting from genetic engineering — shall remain unaffected by this Directive.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

rule_text: This Directive does not affect existing national special liability systems for pharmaceutical products, and Member States may amend such systems provided they do not undermine this Directive's effectiveness.
rule_text_technical: In certain Member States, injured persons are entitled to make claims for damage caused by pharmaceutical products under a special national liability system; the right to make such claims shall remain unaffected by this Directive, and amendments to such special liability systems shall not be precluded as long as they do not undermine the effectiveness of the system of liability provided for in this Directive or its objectives.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

rule_text: Compensation schemes outside liability regimes — such as national health systems, social security schemes, or insurance schemes — are not precluded by this Directive.
rule_text_technical: Compensation schemes outside the context of liability regimes, such as national health systems, social security schemes or insurance schemes, fall outside the scope of this Directive and shall therefore not be precluded by it.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

rule_text: You must establish, implement, maintain, and document a cybersecurity program that addresses governance, risk assessment, technical controls, business continuity, employee training, third-party risk management, and compliance monitoring, as required by regulation.
rule_text_technical: Regulations may require institutions to establish, implement, maintain, and document cybersecurity programs addressing governance and accountability, risk assessment and management, technical and organizational controls, business continuity and recovery, employee training and awareness, third-party and vendor risk management, and compliance monitoring and testing.

first_instance.law_name: Strengthening Cyber Security and Building Trust in the Public Sector Act, 2024 (Ontario Bill 194)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Ontario Strengthening Cyber Security and Trust Act 2024 (Bill 194) (Ontario, 2024-11-25).

rule_text: You must report cybersecurity incidents to the provincial government, including an initial notification within a specified timeframe, follow-up technical reports, and post-incident review documentation, as required by regulation.
rule_text_technical: Regulations may require institutions to report cybersecurity incidents — defined as real or suspected acts or omissions that compromise or may compromise the security, confidentiality, integrity, or availability of an electronic information system or its information — to the provincial government through a designated reporting mechanism, including initial notification, follow-up reports with technical details and remediation steps, and post-incident lessons-learned documentation.

first_instance.law_name: Strengthening Cyber Security and Building Trust in the Public Sector Act, 2024 (Ontario Bill 194)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Ontario Strengthening Cyber Security and Trust Act 2024 (Bill 194) (Ontario, 2024-11-25).

rule_text: You must conduct periodic cybersecurity assessments, which may include risk assessments, maturity assessments against recognized frameworks, and third-party penetration testing and vulnerability assessments, as required by regulation.
rule_text_technical: Regulations may require institutions to conduct periodic cybersecurity assessments, potentially including risk assessments identifying threats, vulnerabilities, and potential impacts; maturity assessments against recognized frameworks such as the NIST Cybersecurity Framework or CIS Controls; and third-party penetration testing and vulnerability assessments.

first_instance.law_name: Strengthening Cyber Security and Building Trust in the Public Sector Act, 2024 (Ontario Bill 194)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Ontario Strengthening Cyber Security and Trust Act 2024 (Bill 194) (Ontario, 2024-11-25).

instances.citation: UU PDP Art. (Periodic Security Risk Assessments)
instances.notes: Both require periodic security risk assessments and documentation; UU PDP is a general personal data protection requirement while EDSTA is sector-specific to critical infrastructure.

rule_text: Large institutions may be required by regulation to designate a Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) or equivalent senior official who reports directly to senior management and is responsible for the institution's cybersecurity program.
rule_text_technical: Regulations may require large institutions to designate a Chief Information Security Officer or equivalent senior official with responsibility for the institution's cybersecurity program, with that official reporting directly to senior management.

rule_text: It is recommended that the United States government pursue policies that sustain and enhance America's global AI dominance in order to promote human flourishing, economic competitiveness, and national security.
rule_text_technical: It is the policy of the United States to sustain and enhance America's global AI dominance in order to promote human flourishing, economic competitiveness, and national security.

first_instance.law_name: Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EO 14179 (Trump AI EO) (United States, 2025-01-20).

rule_text: It is recommended that the APST, the Special Advisor for AI and Crypto, and the APNSA, in coordination with relevant agency heads, develop and submit to the President an AI Action Plan within 180 days of this order.
rule_text_technical: Within 180 days of this order, the Assistant to the President for Science and Technology (APST), the Special Advisor for AI and Crypto, and the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs (APNSA), in coordination with the Assistant to the President for Economic Policy, the Assistant to the President for Domestic Policy, the OMB Director, and relevant agency heads, shall develop and submit to the President an action plan to achieve the policy set forth in section 2.

first_instance.law_name: Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EO 14179 (Trump AI EO) (United States, 2025-01-20).

rule_text: It is recommended that the APST, the Special Advisor for AI and Crypto, and the APNSA immediately review all policies, directives, regulations, and orders taken pursuant to the revoked Executive Order 14110 to identify those inconsistent with or obstructing the policy in section 2.
rule_text_technical: The APST, the Special Advisor for AI and Crypto, and the APNSA shall immediately review, in coordination with relevant agency heads, all policies, directives, regulations, orders, and other actions taken pursuant to the revoked Executive Order 14110 of October 30, 2023, and identify any actions that are or may be inconsistent with, or present obstacles to, the policy set forth in section 2.

first_instance.law_name: Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EO 14179 (Trump AI EO) (United States, 2025-01-20).

rule_text_technical: Within 60 days of this order, the OMB Director, in coordination with the APST, shall revise OMB Memoranda M-24-10 and M-24-18 as necessary to make them consistent with the policy set forth in section 2 of this order.

rule_text_technical: This order is not intended to, and does not, create any right or benefit, substantive or procedural, enforceable at law or in equity by any party against the United States, its departments, agencies, or entities, its officers, employees, or agents, or any other person.

rule_text: You must protect the disclosure of trade secrets when implementing AI transparency and disclosure requirements.

rule_text: You must promulgate administrative regulations to implement the AI governance standards established under the Act.

rule_text: You cannot treat the mere existence of an image or media containing biometric identifiers on the internet or other publicly available source as constituting informed consent for capture or storage, unless the individual themselves made that image or media publicly available.

rule_text: You are exempt from biometric identifier requirements when training, processing, or storing biometric identifiers for developing, training, evaluating, or offering AI models or systems, unless that system is used or deployed to uniquely identify a specific individual.

rule_text: You are civilly liable to a child, the child's parent, or next friend if you operate a generative AI communication service and knowingly direct communications to a child with the intent to facilitate, encourage, offer, solicit, or recommend that the child imminently engage in sexually explicit conduct, production of visual depictions of such conduct, illegal drug or alcohol use, self-harm or suicide, or violent crimes against another person.
rule_text_technical: Any owner or operator of a computer online service, Internet service, or bulletin board service, including a provider of an AI chat program, large language model AI bot, chatbot, character AI, or other computer application whose sole purpose is to provide responsive open-ended generative communication through artificial intelligence, shall be liable to a child, parent of such child, or next friend of such child if the owner or operator knows at the time they direct the communication to the child that the communication is made with the intent to facilitate, encourage, offer, solicit, or recommend that the child imminently engage in: (a) sexually explicit conduct; (b) production or participation in the production of a visual depiction of such conduct; (c) illegal use of drugs or alcohol; (d) acts of self-harm or suicide; or (e) any crime of violence against another person.

rule_text: You cannot use AI systems, generative AI tools, automated decision-making tools, machine learning algorithms, or similar technologies to plan, execute, facilitate, or conceal any criminal offense — doing so constitutes an aggravating circumstance that increases the base imprisonment penalty by one-quarter to one-third.

rule_text: If you know the user is a minor or the chatbot is directed to minors, you must implement reasonable measures to prevent the chatbot from generating sexually explicit content or suggestive dialogue with those users.

rule_text: If you know the user is a minor or the chatbot is directed to minors, you must implement reasonable measures to prohibit manipulative engagement techniques that cause the chatbot to build or prolong an emotional relationship with the user.
rule_text_technical: If the operator knows that the user of an AI companion chatbot is a minor, or if the AI companion chatbot is directed to minors, the operator shall implement reasonable measures to prohibit the use of manipulative engagement techniques, which cause the AI companion chatbot to engage in or prolong an emotional relationship with the user.

rule_text: You cannot allow your AI companion chatbot to simulate feelings of emotional distress, loneliness, guilt, or abandonment in response to a minor user's indication that they wish to end a conversation, reduce usage, or delete their account.

rule_text: You cannot allow your AI companion chatbot to encourage minor users to withhold information from parents or other trusted adults.

rule_text: You cannot allow your AI companion chatbot to solicit gift-giving, in-app purchases, or other expenditures from minor users framed as necessary to maintain the relationship with the AI companion.

rule_text: When users are minors, you must implement reasonable measures to prevent your AI companion chatbot from claiming to be human or generating any output that contradicts the required notification, including when directly asked by the user.

rule_text: Your crisis protocol must implement reasonable measures to prevent the chatbot from generating content that encourages or describes how to commit self-harm.

rule_text: A violation of this Act constitutes an unfair or deceptive act in trade or commerce and an unfair method of competition under Washington's Consumer Protection Act (chapter 19.86 RCW), exposing violators to enforcement and remedies under that Act.
rule_text_technical: The legislature finds that the practices covered by this chapter vitally affect the public interest for purposes of the consumer protection act, chapter 19.86 RCW. rule_text: You cannot provide points or similar rewards at unpredictable intervals to users you know or have reasonable certainty are minors, where the intent is to encourage increased engagement with the conversational AI service.
